fact: Many decisions arise via the accumulation of noisy evidence to a threshold or bound.
source_span: Many decisions are thought to arise via the accumulation of noisy evidence to a threshold or bound .
selection_reasoning: This background fact explains the fundamental decision-making mechanism studied in the article.

fact: In perception, the accumulation of noisy evidence explains how stimulus strength affects decision speed, accuracy, and confidence.
source_span: In perception , the mechanism explains the effect of stimulus strength , characterized by signal-to-noise ratio , on decision speed , accuracy and confidence .
selection_reasoning: This fact provides context for why the study focuses on noise and its effects on decision variables.

fact: An increase in noise should lead to faster decisions, reduced accuracy, and paradoxically, higher confidence according to bounded evidence accumulation models.
source_span: An increase in noise should lead to faster decisions , reduced accuracy and , paradoxically , higher confidence .
selection_reasoning: This is a key theoretical prediction that the study aims to test.

fact: The study introduced a novel sensory manipulation that mimics adding unbiased noise to motion-selective regions of visual cortex.
source_span: To test these predictions , we introduce a novel sensory manipulation that mimics the addition of unbiased noise to motion-selective regions of visual cortex , which we verified with neuronal recordings from macaque areas MT/MST .
selection_reasoning: This describes the main experimental approach used to test the model predictions.

fact: Neuronal recordings from macaque areas MT/MST verified the sensory manipulation increased noise in motion-selective visual cortex.
source_span: which we verified with neuronal recordings from macaque areas MT/MST .
selection_reasoning: This supports the validity of the sensory manipulation method.

fact: In both humans and monkeys, increasing noise induced faster decisions and greater confidence over a range of stimuli with minimal impairment to accuracy.
source_span: For both humans and monkeys , increasing the noise induced faster decisions and greater confidence over a range of stimuli for which accuracy was minimally impaired .
selection_reasoning: This is a principal empirical finding confirming the model's predictions.

fact: The magnitude of the effects of noise on decision speed and confidence matched predictions of a bounded evidence accumulation model.
source_span: The magnitude of the effects was in agreement with predictions of a bounded evidence accumulation model .
selection_reasoning: This fact links the experimental results to the theoretical framework.

fact: Decisions that combine information from different sources or across time serve as a model of cognitive function because they are not hard wired or reflexive but experimentally tractable.
source_span: Decisions that combine information from different sources or across time are of special interest to neuroscience because they serve as a model of cognitive function . These decisions are not hard wired or reflexive , yet they are experimentally tractable .
selection_reasoning: This explains the significance of studying such decisions in neuroscience.

fact: Psychologists have sought to understand how decision formation gives rise to choice, reaction time, and decision confidence.
source_span: Psychologists have long sought to understand how the process of decision formation gives rise to three key observables ... First there is the choice itself ... Second , there is the time it takes to reach a decision ... Third , decisions are often accompanied by a graded degree of belief in the accuracy or appropriateness of the choice . This belief , referred to as decision confidence ...
selection_reasoning: This background fact defines the key observables the study addresses.

fact: Bounded evidence accumulation models explain choice, reaction time, and confidence by depicting decision-making as a race between accumulators integrating momentary evidence until a threshold is reached.
source_span: The family of bounded evidence accumulation models ... depicts the decision process as a race between competing accumulators , each of which integrates momentary evidence for one alternative and against the others . The decision terminates when the accumulated evidence for one alternative , termed a decision variable ( DV ) , reaches a threshold or bound , thereby determining both the choice and the decision time . Confidence in the decision derives from a mapping between the DV and the probability that a decision based on this DV will be correct .
selection_reasoning: This fact summarizes the theoretical framework central to the study.

fact: Noise in momentary evidence causes the decision variable to fluctuate, influencing reaction time and confidence especially when signal-to-noise ratio is low.
source_span: The noisiness of the momentary evidence causes the DV to wander from its starting point , as in Brownian motion or diffusion ... Noise is the main determinant of both RT and confidence when signal-to-noise is low , that is when choices are more stochastic ( less accurate ) .
selection_reasoning: This explains the role of noise in decision dynamics, motivating the experimental manipulation.

fact: If noise is selectively increased without changing the expectation of momentary evidence, bounded accumulation predicts lower accuracy with strong evidence, faster reaction times with weak evidence, and increased confidence with weak evidence.
source_span: Specifically , were it possible to leave unchanged the expectation of each sample of momentary evidence while boosting the noise associated with it , then the bounded accumulation of the noisier samples should lead to ( i ) lower accuracy when the expectation of the momentary evidence is strong , ( ii ) faster reaction times when the momentary evidence is weak , and ( iii ) increased confidence when the momentary evidence is weak .
selection_reasoning: This outlines the specific testable predictions that the study addresses.

fact: The study introduced a method to selectively increase the variance (volatility) of motion evidence in a random dot motion display without changing its mean motion strength.
source_span: We therefore sought a method to manipulate the variance associated with the neural representation of momentary evidence without affecting its mean. We achieved this with a manipulation of the motion information in a random dot motion (RDM) display, by adding a second level of randomness which increased its volatility but was unbiased with respect to the strength and direction of motion evidence.
selection_reasoning: This fact describes the key methodological innovation central to the study's main question and experimental design.

fact: Neurons in the middle temporal (MT) and medial superior temporal (MST) areas of the macaque visual cortex represent momentary motion evidence and were used to verify the volatility manipulation.
source_span: We verified that the manipulation has the desired properties by recording from direction selective neurons in the middle temporal (MT) and medial superior temporal (MST) areas of the macaque visual cortex. Neurons in these areas are known to represent the momentary evidence in tasks identical to those in our study.
selection_reasoning: This fact provides important biological context and validation of the manipulation at the neural level, supporting the study's claims.

fact: The volatility manipulation increased the variance of motion evidence and neural responses without significantly changing the mean motion strength or mean neural response.
source_span: For all motion strengths, the mean (upper) is not affected by the volatility manipulation, whereas the variance is larger in the high volatility condition. The volatility manipulation produced a small increase in the average firing rate at the low coherences (upper)... The variance parallels the mean, but volatility has a more marked effect on variance at weak motion strengths.
selection_reasoning: This fact captures the principal finding that the manipulation selectively increased noise (variance) while keeping the mean evidence stable, which is central to testing the study hypothesis.

fact: The study tested how increased noise (volatility) in motion evidence affects choice behavior measures including accuracy, reaction time, and confidence in both monkeys and humans.
source_span: We then used the volatility manipulation to test the influence of noise on the three observables of choice behavior—accuracy, RT and confidence—in monkeys and humans.
selection_reasoning: This fact states the main behavioral question and the cross-species approach, which is core to the study's significance.

fact: Previous studies suggested that increased neural noise can dissociate accuracy from confidence, but lacked a controlled method to selectively increase noise without affecting mean evidence.
source_span: These predictions have not been tested thoroughly, because a controlled method for selectively increasing noise is not known. A dissociation between accuracy and confidence led Rahnev et al. (2012) to conclude that transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) increased the neural noise associated with the representation of a visual pattern... However, characterization of these effects of TMS and µStim was inferred from behavior.
selection_reasoning: This fact provides background motivation explaining why the current study's method and question are important.

fact: The variance of neural responses to motion stimuli increases more under high volatility conditions, especially at low motion strengths.
source_span: The variance of the neural response is known to scale approximately linearly with firing rate ( Tolhurst et al., 1983; Vogels et al., 1989; Geisler and Albrecht, 1997; Shadlen and Newsome, 1998 ). Thus the variance curves in Figure 2C ( lower panel ) parallel the means. The high volatility condition adds to the variance in a manner that is exaggerated at the low motion strengths, consistent with the motion energy analysis above.
selection_reasoning: This fact highlights a key finding about how stimulus volatility affects neural variability, which is central to understanding neural processing of motion and decision-making.

fact: The firing rate of direction-selective neurons in cortical areas MT/MST increases linearly with motion strength in the preferred direction and decreases less steeply in the anti-preferred direction, forming a bilinear function.
source_span: As previously shown ( Britten et al., 1993 ), the firing rate of MT neurons increases linearly, on average, as a function of motion strength in the neuron’s preferred direction ( c > 0, Figure 2C, upper panel, blue trace ). The firing rate decreases linearly, but less steeply, as a function of motion strength in the anti-preferred direction ( c < 0 ), giving rise to a bilinear function.
selection_reasoning: This background fact defines the neural response pattern to motion strength, which is fundamental to interpreting the effects of volatility on neural signals.

fact: High volatility stimuli increase the variance of motion energy compared to low volatility stimuli, especially at low motion coherences.
source_span: A more systematic analysis of the motion energy, displayed in Figure 2B, reveals that the mean is identical for low and high volatility stimuli, for all motion strengths ( upper panel ), whereas the variance is larger for the high volatility stimuli ( lower panel ). ... Note that the effect is strongest at the low coherences, where the distribution of c in the high volatility condition spans both positive and negative values.
selection_reasoning: This fact describes how stimulus volatility affects the sensory input variability, which is key to understanding the neural and behavioral consequences.

fact: The momentary evidence used by monkeys to guide motion discrimination decisions is represented by the difference in firing rates between two pools of neurons preferring opposite motion directions.
source_span: We assume that the momentary evidence is the difference between the average firing rates from two pools of neurons with direction preferences for the two opposite directions ( e.g., right-preferring minus left-preferring ) ( Shadlen et al., 1996; Ditterich et al., 2003 ).
selection_reasoning: This fact explains the neural mechanism underlying decision formation, which is central to the study's question.

fact: The visual system blurs rapidly displayed random dot motion stimuli over time, creating an illusion of more dots present simultaneously than are actually displayed.
source_span: The construction of the RDM we use is in video frames displayed every 1/75 of a second. The visual system blurs these images over time, leading for example to the illusion that many more dots are present simultaneously than are actually displayed.
selection_reasoning: This background fact helps explain the nature of the stimulus and why it is relevant for studying motion perception.

fact: An established motion filter applied to the stimuli extracts a time-blurred motion signal that approximates the firing rates of direction-selective neurons in primate visual cortex.
source_span: The right panel of Figure 2A applies an established motion filter ( Adelson and Bergen, 1985 ) to the example movies parameterized by the low and high volatility traces shown in the left panel ( see also Video 1 ). The filter extracts a time-blurred motion signal that provides a reasonable approximation to the firing rates of direction selective neurons in the primate visual cortex ( Britten et al., 1993; Rust et al., 2006; Hedges et al., 2011 ).
selection_reasoning: This fact describes a key method used to relate stimulus properties to neural responses, important for interpreting results.

fact: The mean motion energy is identical for low and high volatility stimuli across all motion strengths.
source_span: A more systematic analysis of the motion energy, displayed in Figure 2B, reveals that the mean is identical for low and high volatility stimuli, for all motion strengths ( upper panel ).
selection_reasoning: This fact establishes that volatility affects variance but not mean motion energy, a critical distinction for understanding stimulus effects.

fact: The study investigated how changes in the variance of momentary sensory evidence affect decision speed, accuracy, and confidence in a motion direction discrimination task.
source_span: In what follows we attempt to ascertain whether a change in the variance of the momentary evidence , introduced by our volatility manipulation , affects decision speed , accuracy , and confidence in accordance with the predictions of bounded evidence accumulation .
selection_reasoning: This fact states the main research question and motivation, which is central to the abstract-level summary.

fact: One monkey and three human subjects performed a task requiring them to decide the direction of motion in a dynamic random dot display by making a saccadic eye movement to one of two targets.
source_span: One monkey ( monkey W ) and three humans were required to decide between two possible directions of motion and , when ready , to indicate their decision by looking to one of two targets ( Figure 3A ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact describes the key experimental subjects and task, important for understanding the study design.

fact: Stronger motion coherence led to faster and more accurate choices in both high and low volatility conditions.
source_span: For both high and low volatility conditions , stronger motion led to faster and more accurate choices .
selection_reasoning: This fact summarizes a principal behavioral finding relevant to the study's context.

fact: Increasing stimulus volatility increased the variance of momentary evidence, especially at low motion strengths, without substantially changing the mean evidence.
source_span: From these complementary analyses of stimulus and neural response , we conclude that the volatility manipulation has negligible effects on the expectation of momentary evidence and more substantial effects on the variance , especially at weak motion strengths .
selection_reasoning: This fact links the stimulus manipulation to its neural effect, a key mechanistic insight.

fact: High volatility decreased reaction times, particularly at the weakest motion strengths, across all subjects.
source_span: The main effect of high volatility was to decrease RTs , particularly at the weakest motion strengths ( Figure 3B , bottom row , red ) . This effect was robust for all three human subjects and the monkey ( Equation 16 , all p<0 . 03 , t-test , H0: β2=0 ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact reports a principal behavioral effect of the volatility manipulation, central to the study's conclusions.

fact: The effect of high volatility on accuracy was subtle and not statistically reliable for individual subjects in the reaction time task but was significant when pooling data across subjects and including confidence tasks.
source_span: The manipulation affected the accuracy only subtly , and this was not statistically reliable for individual subjects in the RT task ( Figure 3B , top row; for the four subjects: p=[0 . 35 , 0 . 65 , 0 . 2 , 0 . 26] , Equation 17 , likelihood-ratio test ) . However , there was a significant effect of volatility on accuracy when pooling data across subjects and including data from the confidence tasks described below ( Equation 18 , p<0 . 0005 , likelihood ratio test , H0: β2=0; see also Figure 3—figure supplement 1 ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact captures nuanced findings about accuracy, important for a balanced summary of behavioral effects.

fact: The momentary evidence was modeled as the difference between average firing rates of two pools of neurons with opposite direction preferences in area MT.
source_span: We assume that the momentary evidence is the difference between the average firing rates from two pools of neurons with direction preferences for the two opposite directions ( e . g . , right-preferring minus left-preferring ) ( Shadlen et al . , 1996; Ditterich et al . , 2003; Hanks et al . , 2006 ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact provides a key mechanistic assumption linking neural activity to decision evidence, important for understanding the study's theoretical framework.

fact: Subjects decided the net direction of motion in a dynamic random dot display by making a saccadic eye movement to the corresponding target.
source_span: Subjects reported their decision by making a saccadic eye movement to the right ( left ) target for rightward ( leftward ) motion.
selection_reasoning: This describes the core behavioral task used to measure decision-making, which is central to the study.

fact: High volatility in the motion stimulus had only weak effects on choice accuracy but significantly shortened reaction times, especially at low motion strengths.
source_span: High volatility had only weak effects on accuracy ( upper ) but shortened the reaction times for all subjects ( lower ) , particularly at the low motion strengths.
selection_reasoning: This is a principal finding about how stimulus volatility affects decision speed and accuracy.

fact: Decisions are consistent with a bounded evidence accumulation model where noisy evidence is integrated until reaching a decision bound.
source_span: The pattern of results in Figure 3B is consistent with the hypothesis that decisions are made when an accumulation of noisy evidence reaches a bound.
selection_reasoning: This provides the key theoretical framework explaining the decision process studied.

fact: Increased stimulus volatility increases the variance of momentary evidence, which accelerates the decision variable's movement toward decision bounds, leading to faster reaction times.
source_span: The volatility manipulation mainly affects the weakest motion strengths where accuracy is already poor... by increasing noise, the volatility manipulation accelerates the dispersion of the decision variable away from its expected value and nearer the termination bounds, hence faster RT.
selection_reasoning: This explains the mechanism by which volatility affects decision speed, a core mechanistic insight.

fact: Confidence in a decision can be formalized as the conditional probability that the choice is correct given the accumulated evidence and elapsed decision time.
source_span: Confidence refers to the belief that a decision one is about to make ( or has just made ) is likely to be correct. In the framework of bounded evidence accumulation, it can be formalized as the conditional probability of a correct choice given the state of the DV, which comprises the accumulated evidence and elapsed decision time.
selection_reasoning: This defines confidence in the context of the study, important for understanding subsequent findings.

fact: Increased volatility is predicted to increase confidence at low motion coherences by accelerating the decision variable away from neutral values.
source_span: Increased volatility should affect confidence because it mimics an increase in the diffusion rate. At low coherences in particular, its main effect on the DV is to accelerate its exodus away from neutral ( probability correct = 0.5 ) to more extreme values. Therefore, we predicted that volatility would increase confidence at low coherences.
selection_reasoning: This is a key hypothesis linking volatility to confidence, central to the study's question.

fact: A monkey was trained on a motion discrimination task with post-decision wagering, allowing it to opt out of difficult decisions for a smaller but certain reward.
source_span: Monkey D was trained on a motion discrimination task with post-decision wagering... On half of the trials, the monkey had the opportunity to opt out of reporting the direction choice and to select instead a smaller but certain reward.
selection_reasoning: This describes a key experimental method used to measure confidence behaviorally.

fact: The high volatility random dot motion stimulus was introduced on a random half of trials after extensive experience with the low volatility stimulus.
source_span: After extensive experience with the standard RDM ( >100,000 trials; low volatility condition ), we introduced the high volatility RDM on a random half of the trials.
selection_reasoning: This details the experimental manipulation critical to testing the effects of volatility.

fact: The study investigated how high volatility in a random dot motion (RDM) task affects decision confidence and choice behavior in monkeys.
source_span: The main question we wished to address is whether the high volatility condition would elicit fewer sure-bet choices, consistent with greater confidence.
selection_reasoning: This fact states the core research question motivating the study, essential for understanding the study's purpose.

fact: Monkeys performed a direction discrimination task where they indicated motion direction by eye movement and could opt for a sure-bet option that gave a small but certain reward.
source_span: The monkey viewed the motion display for random duration, controlled by the computer, followed by a memory-delay period. When the fixation point was extinguished, the monkey indicated the net direction of motion by making an eye movement to a left or right choice target in order to receive a liquid reward, if correct. On a random half of trials, the monkey was presented a third ‘sure bet’ option (red target) during the delay period, which if chosen resulted in a small but certain reward.
selection_reasoning: This describes the key behavioral task and the sure-bet option, which is central to measuring decision confidence.

fact: High volatility in the motion stimulus increased the monkey’s confidence, as shown by a greater tendency to waive the sure-bet option and make a direction choice.
source_span: As shown in Figure 4B (lower panel), the proportion of trials the monkey decided to waive the sure-bet option (deciding instead for a riskier direction choice) was greater on the high volatility trials (Equation 19, p<10–6, likelihood-ratio test). Thus, high volatility increased the monkey’s confidence, and did so despite a negligible effect on accuracy (Figure 4B, upper).
selection_reasoning: This is a principal finding linking stimulus volatility to increased confidence without affecting accuracy.

fact: Volatility affected decision confidence mainly at weak and intermediate motion strengths, where the evidence was less clear.
source_span: The effect was concentrated at weak and intermediate motion strengths.
selection_reasoning: This detail clarifies the conditions under which volatility influences confidence, important for interpreting the results.

fact: Monkeys made rational use of the sure-bet option by opting out more often when motion evidence was weak or stimulus duration was brief, improving accuracy on trials where they chose a direction.
source_span: In both low and high volatility conditions, the monkey made rational use of the sure bet, opting out more often for weaker motion (Equation 19, p<10–6, logistic regression) and for briefer stimuli (Equation 19, p<10–6, logistic regression). When the sure bet was offered but waived, choice accuracy was higher than when the sure bet was not offered (Equation 20, p<10–6, logistic regression).
selection_reasoning: This shows the monkey’s adaptive behavior in using the sure-bet option, supporting the interpretation of confidence.

fact: The decision to accept or waive the sure-bet option was based on the state of the evidence on each trial rather than a fixed bias associated with motion strength.
source_span: It implies that the decision to accept or waive the sure bet is based on the state of the evidence on the trial and not a general propensity associated with each motion strength (Kiani and Shadlen, 2009).
selection_reasoning: This clarifies the mechanism underlying the monkey’s confidence judgments, relevant to the study’s interpretation.

fact: Human participants showed a similar effect of volatility on confidence, reporting higher confidence ratings for high volatility stimuli, especially at low coherence levels.
source_span: The results from the human observers were similar to those from the monkey. ... They also reported higher confidence for the high volatility stimuli, and the effect was most apparent for the low coherence stimuli (Equation 21, p<0.0004, t-test).
selection_reasoning: This extends the main finding to humans, supporting the generality and significance of the results.

fact: Volatility did not systematically affect accuracy in either monkeys or human participants.
source_span: Volatility did not affect accuracy systematically (upper panels).
selection_reasoning: This fact highlights that confidence changes were not due to changes in actual performance, an important distinction.

fact: In the human task, participants reported their direction choice and confidence simultaneously by gaze position on targets, encouraging use of all available stimulus information.
source_span: Participants reported the choice and the confidence rating by looking at a particular position on one of two elongated targets (Figure 5A), where the left or right target specified the motion choice and the vertical position was used to indicate confidence. They were allowed to adjust their gaze to the desired level before finalizing their combined choice and confidence report.
selection_reasoning: This describes the key method used to measure confidence in humans, relevant to understanding the human data.

fact: A single bounded accumulation model can explain how motion strength and volatility affect choice, accuracy, reaction time, and confidence in perceptual decisions.
source_span: So far, the effect of volatility has been described qualitatively. Now we show how a single bounded accumulation model can account for the combined effect of motion strength and volatility on choice, accuracy and RT.
selection_reasoning: This fact summarizes the main modeling approach used to explain key behavioral effects, central to the study's principal findings.

fact: In the bounded accumulation model, choice, reaction time, and confidence result from accumulating noisy momentary evidence until a decision bound is reached or the stimulus ends.
source_span: In the model, choice, RT and confidence result from the accumulation of noisy momentary evidence as a function of time, until the integral of the evidence (the decision variable, DV) reaches one of two bounds, or for the PDW and confidence tasks, until the stimulus is curtailed.
selection_reasoning: This fact describes the core mechanism underlying the model, important for understanding how decisions and confidence are generated.

fact: The variance of momentary evidence increases with motion strength, and the difference in noise between volatility conditions is largest at zero coherence and decreases with stronger motion.
source_span: These analyses showed that (i) the variance of the momentary evidence increases with motion strength, and (ii) the difference in noise between volatility conditions is larger at 0% coherence and decays gradually for stronger motion.
selection_reasoning: This fact captures a key empirical observation about how stimulus properties affect evidence noise, which is central to the model's parameterization and findings.

fact: The model assumes that the brain has implicit knowledge of the accumulated evidence state, elapsed decision time, and how these map to the probability of making a correct choice to explain confidence judgments.
source_span: We assume that the brain has implicit knowledge of (i) the state of the accumulated evidence, (ii) the elapsed deliberation time, and (iii) the mapping of time and evidence to the probability of making a correct choice.
selection_reasoning: This fact explains the theoretical basis for how confidence is computed, a principal conceptual claim.

fact: The model's predictions capture human confidence ratings well, supporting that time and accumulated evidence are main determinants of confidence even when noise is experimentally controlled.
source_span: These predictions capture the trend well, supporting the notion that time and accumulated evidence are the main determinants of confidence in a perceptual choice, even when noise is under experimental control.
selection_reasoning: This fact states a key validation of the model against human data, a principal finding.

fact: The influence of motion strength and volatility on choice, reaction time, and confidence can be explained by a common bounded evidence accumulation mechanism across tasks and species.
source_span: The overall quality of the fits—across all tasks and both species—indicates that the influence of motion strength and volatility on choice, reaction time and confidence can be explained by a common mechanism of bounded evidence accumulation.
selection_reasoning: This fact highlights the generality and significance of the model's explanatory power, a key conclusion.

fact: Many previous studies assumed that the variance of momentary evidence is fixed and independent of motion strength, but this study shows that variance increases with motion strength due to partial rectification in neural responses.
source_span: Many studies make the simplifying assumption that the variance of the momentary evidence is fixed and independent of motion strength... However, the partial rectification implies that the variance of the difference should increase as a function of motion strength.
selection_reasoning: This fact provides important background and motivation for the study's novel modeling approach.

fact: Subjects apply the same mapping between accumulated evidence and confidence regardless of stimulus volatility condition.
source_span: that subjects apply the same mapping between the accumulated evidence ( the DV ) and the probability that a decision rendered upon that evidence will be correct ( i . e . , confidence ) , regardless of the volatility condition .
selection_reasoning: This is a core finding about how confidence is computed across different volatility conditions, central to the study's main question.

fact: Models assuming subjects have full and immediate knowledge of volatility and use separate mappings for each volatility condition fit the data worse than a common mapping model.
source_span: When fit to data , this two-map model produces visibly worse fits than the model that relies on a common map , despite having the same number of parameters ( Figure 6B; ∆BIC = 252 . 4 favoring the common-map model; see Table 2 for parameter fits ) .
selection_reasoning: This finding supports the conclusion that subjects do not adjust confidence mappings based on volatility, a key result.

fact: A model where subjects gradually infer volatility during a trial fits the data similarly to the common mapping model but estimates a very slow rate of volatility identification.
source_span: For the second two-map model , the assessment of volatility is not instantaneous but evolves over the course of a trial . ... the rate estimated from the best fit is exceedingly slow . For example , after 1 s of viewing , the weight assigned to the appropriate volatility map is just 1% . ... The fit is indistinguishable from the common-map model depicted in Figure 4 ( see Table 2 ) , and the BIC statistic revealed that the addition of the extra parameter was not justified ( ∆BIC = 7 . 24 ) .
selection_reasoning: This result indicates that even if volatility is inferred, it does not substantially affect confidence mapping, reinforcing the main conclusion.

fact: Allowing different decision bounds for high and low volatility conditions does not improve model fits compared to a common bound model.
source_span: We also considered the possibility that subjects used different termination criteria ( bound heights ) on low and high volatility trials . ... This model was also inferior to the simpler common-map model ( ∆BIC = 127; see Table 2 for parameter fits ) . ... We also fit a model for the RT task that allowed the bounds to be different for the two volatility conditions . This led to a marginal increase in the likelihoods , but not enough to justify the addition of the extra parameter ( ∆BIC = [29 . 4 , 7 . 7 , 27 . 3 , 12 . 1] for the four subjects; Table 2 ) .
selection_reasoning: This supports the conclusion that subjects do not adjust decision criteria based on volatility, a key aspect of the study's findings.

fact: The study's volatility manipulation was validated and characterized using neural data from neurons known to represent momentary evidence for decisions and confidence.
source_span: The role of the neural data in this study was to validate and characterize the volatility manipulation in a population of neurons known to represent the momentary evidence used to inform decisions and confidence ( Salzman et al . , 1990; Ditterich
selection_reasoning: This provides important background and methodological context linking neural evidence to the behavioral findings.

fact: Subjects likely do not infer or revise their confidence mapping based on the noisiness of incoming evidence during the task.
source_span: Thus , we assume that subjects do not infer the noisiness of incoming evidence , or that if they do , they do not revise the mapping accordingly .
selection_reasoning: This assumption underpins the modeling approach and interpretation of the results, relevant for understanding the study's conclusions.

fact: The normative strategy for similar decision tasks would apply different decision bounds and mappings for different volatility conditions, but subjects in this study did not follow this strategy.
source_span: Indeed , the normative strategy for several model tasks , which approximate those in our study , would apply different bounds and mappings to the two volatility conditions ( see Appendix ) . The full normative solution for the tasks we used is not known . source_span: The role of the neural data in this study was to validate and characterize the volatility manipulation in a population of neurons known to represent the momentary evidence used to inform decisions and confidence ( Salzman et al . , 1990; Ditterich et al . , 2003; Hanks et al . , 2006; Fetsch et al . , 2014 ) .
selection_reasoning: This explains the purpose of the neural recordings and their relevance to the study's main question.

fact: Trial-to-trial variation in the activity of neurons in MT/MST was indicative of the monkey's upcoming choice in both low and high volatility conditions.
source_span: Consistent with earlier reports ( Britten et al . , 1992 ) , trial to trial variation in the activity of neurons in MT/MST were indicative of the choice that the monkey was about to make . For both low and high volatility conditions , trial-to-trial variation in the neural response was reflected in the monkey’s choices .
selection_reasoning: This is a principal finding linking neural activity to decision-making under different volatility conditions.

fact: Neural fluctuations were more informative in the high volatility condition, likely due to increased variance in the motion stimulus.
source_span: The fluctuations were more informative in the high volatility condition , presumably because they were induced by exaggerated variance in the motion display itself ( e . g . , Figure 2A ) .
selection_reasoning: This finding connects the experimental manipulation (volatility) to neural response differences, central to the study.

fact: The time course of choice-related neural signals evolved with similar latencies in low and high volatility conditions, matching the latency of direction-selective signals.
source_span: Notably , the time course of choice-related signals evolved with similar latencies in the low and high volatility conditions . The latencies were comparable to that of the direction selective signal itself ( Figure 7B ) , suggesting that the choice was informed by the earliest motion information available in the stimulus ( Kiani et al . , 2008 ) .
selection_reasoning: This describes a key temporal aspect of neural processing relevant to decision formation.

fact: The influence of neural variation on choice declines over about 200 ms, consistent with the brain terminating some decisions before stimulus end.

selection_reasoning: This finding informs the timing of decision processes, important for understanding neural mechanisms.

fact: Trial-by-trial variation in neural activity was correlated with the monkey's decision to accept or waive a sure-bet option when offered.

selection_reasoning: This links neural signals not only to choice but also to confidence-related decisions, a core study focus.

fact: Momentary evidence for motion direction is proportional to the difference in firing rates between pools of neurons with opposite direction preferences.
source_span: Findings from neurophysiology (Ditterich et al., 2003) and computational modeling (Mazurek et al., 2003) suggest that the momentary evidence is proportional to the difference of firing rates between pools of neurons with opposite direction preferences (e.g., right-preferring minus left-preferring).
selection_reasoning: This fact provides a mechanistic basis for interpreting neural signals in the context of motion direction decisions.

fact: The variance of the difference in firing rates between neuron pools with opposite direction preferences depends on the average pairwise correlation within pools and the correlation between pools.
source_span: Because the variance of a sum equals the sum of the covariances, if the average pairwise correlation for a pool of n neurons is given by r, then the variance of the average response of the pool is (σ2/n + (n−1)rσ2/n). Further, there is a portion of the variance that is shared between neurons tuned to the preferred and anti-preferred directions. If the correlation between the average responses of populations of neurons with opposite directional preferences is given by ρ, the variance of the difference variable is given by Equation 1 of the main text.
selection_reasoning: This fact explains how correlated neural variability influences the reliability of motion evidence signals.

fact: The deamidase OspI from Shigella flexneri modifies a glutamine residue in the host enzyme UBC13 to glutamate, inhibiting its polyubiquitination activity and downstream NF-κB inflammatory response.

To inactivate Nf-κB signaling , Shigella flexneri secretes a Type III effector called OspI , which functions as a deamidase ( Sanada et al . , 2012 ) .
selection_reasoning: This provides motivation and disease context explaining why the bacterial effector targets NF-κB signaling.

fact: UBC13 and the RING-finger ubiquitin ligase TRAF6 work together to synthesize polyubiquitin chains that activate NF-κB signaling in response to inflammatory stimuli.
source_span: In the early events of interleukin-dependent activation of Nf-κB signaling , the Ub-conjugating enzyme UBC13 , and the Ub-ligase TRAF6 function together to synthesize both unanchored polyubiquitin chains , and anchored polyubiquitin chains on TRAF6 and its substrate NEMO ( Chen , 2005 ) . These chains serve as a scaffold to bring together TAK1/2 and IKK kinases , eventually leading to phosphorylation and activation of the IKK kinases , IκB degradation and nuclear translocation of transcription factor Nf-κB .

fact: The granular retrosplenial cortex (RSG) is critical for both spatial and non-spatial behaviors.
source_span: The granular retrosplenial cortex ( RSG ) is critical for both spatial and non-spatial behaviors , but the underlying neural codes remain poorly understood .
selection_reasoning: This background fact explains the importance of the RSG and motivates the study.

fact: The granular retrosplenial cortex (RSG) integrates inputs from multiple cortical and subcortical sources and is part of the brain's default mode network.
source_span: The RSG is also among the most densely connected regions of the brain , integrating inputs from a bevy of cortical and subcortical sources and serving as part of the default mode network ( Greicius et al . , 2009; Kaboodvand et al . , 2018; Liu et al . , 2019; Whitesell et al . , 2021 ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact provides important context about the RSG's connectivity and functional relevance.

fact: The anterior thalamus and dorsal subiculum provide spatial information inputs that selectively recruit low-rheobase (LR) pyramidal cells in the superficial layers of the RSG.
source_span: The anterior thalamus and dorsal subiculum , sources of spatial information , strongly and selectively recruit small low-rheobase ( LR ) pyramidal cells in RSG .
selection_reasoning: This is a key finding about input specificity and cell-type targeting relevant to spatial processing.

fact: Claustral and anterior cingulate inputs, which carry mostly non-spatial information, preferentially control neighboring regular-spiking (RS) pyramidal cells in the superficial RSG.
source_span: In contrast , neighboring regular-spiking ( RS ) cells are preferentially controlled by claustral and anterior cingulate inputs , sources of mostly non-spatial information .
selection_reasoning: This fact complements the previous one, showing parallel processing streams for non-spatial information.

fact: Precise sublaminar axonal and dendritic arborization within layer 1 of the RSG permits parallel processing of spatial and non-spatial inputs.
source_span: Precise sublaminar axonal and dendritic arborization within RSG layer 1 , in particular , permits this parallel processing .
selection_reasoning: This explains the anatomical basis for the functional segregation of inputs.

fact: Thalamocortical synaptic dynamics enable low-rheobase (LR) neurons in the RSG to compute the speed of head rotation despite receiving head direction inputs that do not explicitly encode speed.
source_span: Observed thalamocortical synaptic dynamics enable computational models of LR neurons to compute the speed of head rotation , despite receiving head direction inputs that do not explicitly encode speed .
selection_reasoning: This is a principal mechanistic finding linking synaptic properties to spatial orientation computation.

fact: Parallel input streams identify a distinct principal neuronal subtype, the low-rheobase (LR) neuron, as ideally positioned to support spatial orientation computations in the RSG.
source_span: Thus , parallel input streams identify a distinct principal neuronal subtype ideally positioned to support spatial orientation computations in the RSG .
selection_reasoning: This summarizes the significance of the cell-type specific input segregation for spatial function.

fact: Activity in the granular retrosplenial cortex (RSG) is correlated with a wide variety of behaviors including spatial navigation, learning, memory, fear conditioning, imagination, and planning for the future.
source_span: Activity in the granular retrosplenial cortex ( RSG ) is correlated with a wide variety of behaviors , including spatial navigation , learning , memory , fear conditioning , imagination , and planning for the future ( Alexander et al . , 2020; Alexander and Nitz , 2017; Chang et al . , 2020; Chrastil , 2018; Hinman et al . , 2018; Mao et al . , 2018; Miller et al . , 2021; Miller et al . , 2019 ) .
selection_reasoning: This background fact highlights the broad behavioral relevance of the RSG.

fact: The RSG receives inputs from thalamic nuclei, including the anterior thalamus which contains the highest proportion of head direction cells in the brain.
source_span: Matrix thalamocortical ( TC ) inputs from the anterior thalamus , which contains the highest proportion of head direction cells in the brain ( Taube and Bassett , 2003 ) , influence layer 5 pyramidal cells in RSG ( Yamawaki et al . , 2019b ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact provides important background on the source of spatial information to the RSG.

fact: The RSG receives widespread inputs from the claustrum, which innervates both excitatory and inhibitory neurons via precise laminar targeting.
source_span: The cortex , including the RSG , also receives widespread inputs from the densely connected claustrum ( Brown et al . , 2017; Crick and Koch , 2005; Goll et al . , 2015; Jackson et al . , 2018; Kim et al . , 2016; Narikiyo et al . , 2020; Wang et al . , 2017; White and Mathur , 2018 ) . As with TC signaling , the claustrum innervates both excitatory ( da Costa et al . , 2010; Narikiyo et al . , 2020 ) and inhibitory ( Jackson et al . , 2018; Narikiyo et al . , 2020; Salerno et al . , 1984 ) neurons via precise laminar targeting ( Wang et al . , 2017 ) and projects to many of the same cortical regions as the thalamus ( Burman et al . , 2011 ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact provides background on the claustrum inputs relevant to non-spatial processing.

fact: The RSG receives direct innervation from the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), which is implicated in shared limbic and cognitive functions including fear conditioning.
source_span: The RSG receives direct innervation from the secondary motor cortex ( Yamawaki et al . , 2016a ) , contralateral RSG ( Sempere-Ferràndez et al . , 2018; Wyss et al . , 1990 ) , and anterior cingulate cortex ( ACC; Van Groen and Wyss , 2003; van Groen and Wyss , 1990 ) , among others . The RSG and ACC , in particular , have been implicated in several shared limbic and cognitive functions , including fear conditioning ( Frankland et al . , 2004; Han et al . , 2003; Yamawaki et al . , 2019a; Yamawaki et al . , 2019b ) , but the cellular targets of ACC inputs to RSG have not been identified .
selection_reasoning: This fact provides background on ACC inputs and their functional relevance.

fact: Within the superficial layers of the RSG, two principal excitatory pyramidal neuron subtypes exist: low-rheobase (LR) neurons and regular-spiking (RS) neurons, which differ in physiology, morphology, and computational capabilities.
source_span: Within the RSG , the superficial layers contain two subtypes of principal excitatory pyramidal neurons that have strikingly distinct physiology , morphology , and computational capabilities: the low-rheobase ( LR ) neuron and the regular-spiking ( RS ) neuron ( Brennan et al . , 2020; Kurotani et al . , 2013; Yousuf et al . , 2020 ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact defines the key neuronal subtypes central to the study's findings.

fact: The granular retrosplenial cortex (RSG) contains two types of principal pyramidal neurons in its superficial layers: low-rheobase (LR) neurons and regular-spiking (RS) neurons.
source_span: Layer 3 of the granular retrosplenial cortex ( RSG ) contains two types of principal pyramidal neurons: the low-rheobase ( LR ) neuron and the regular-spiking ( RS ) neuron ( Brennan et al . , 2020; Kurotani et al . , 2013; Yousuf et al . , 2020 ).
selection_reasoning: This background fact defines the key neuronal subtypes studied and is essential to understand the study's focus.

fact: Anterior thalamic inputs to the RSG preferentially target low-rheobase (LR) neurons rather than regular-spiking (RS) neurons.
source_span: LR neurons were strongly driven past spike threshold by these thalamic inputs while RS neurons exhibited far smaller EPSPs ... This suggests that LR neurons receive stronger activation from TC inputs than their neighboring L3 RS neurons.
selection_reasoning: This is a principal finding about the specificity of thalamic inputs to LR neurons, central to the study's main claim.

fact: Claustral and anterior cingulate inputs preferentially target regular-spiking (RS) neurons in the RSG.
source_span: Specifically, we find that anterior thalamus and dorsal subiculum preferentially control LR neurons, whereas claustrum and anterior cingulate control RS cells.
selection_reasoning: This fact complements the double dissociation of inputs to LR and RS neurons, a key mechanistic insight.

fact: The dendrites of LR neurons co-localize with anterior thalamic axons in layer 1a and layer 3 of the RSG, whereas RS neuron dendrites do not.
source_span: Apical dendrites of LR neurons were most densely localized to L1a ... RS apical dendrites rarely entered L1a ... Projection density analysis showed localization of ADAV axons and terminal arbors in L1a and weakly in L3 ... dendrites of LR, but not RS, cells selectively co-localize within layers 1a and 3 with ADAV TC afferents.
selection_reasoning: This anatomical evidence supports the functional specificity of thalamic inputs to LR neurons.

fact: Channelrhodopsin-assisted circuit mapping (CRACM) was used to selectively stimulate inputs from anterior thalamic nuclei to RSG neurons and measure their responses.
source_span: Here, we use channelrhodopsin (ChR2)-assisted circuit mapping (CRACM) to study the subtype-specific circuits formed by anterior thalamic, claustral, anterior cingulate, and dorsal subicular inputs to the RSG.
selection_reasoning: This high-level method description is important to understand how input specificity was experimentally determined.

fact: Synaptic dynamics of anterior thalamic inputs enable LR neurons to robustly encode angular speed despite the inputs only explicitly containing head direction information.
source_span: We show that the synaptic dynamics of thalamic inputs allow for the robust encoding of angular speed by LR cell models, even though these inputs only explicitly contain information about head direction, not speed.
selection_reasoning: This finding links the circuit specificity to a functional role in spatial orientation.

fact: LR neurons are ideally positioned to contribute to initial spatial orientation computations performed in superficial RSG.
source_span: Together, our results suggest that LR neurons are ideally positioned to contribute to the initial spatial orientation computations performed in superficial RSG.
selection_reasoning: This statement highlights the significance and implication of the findings for spatial cognition.

fact: LR neurons in the retrosplenial granular cortex (RSG) receive and process head direction inputs from the anterior thalamus more strongly than layer 3 or 5 regular spiking (RS) neurons.
source_span: This suggests that LR neurons , rather than layer 3 or 5 RS neurons , are the predominant RSG cell type receiving and processing head direction inputs from the anterior thalamus.
selection_reasoning: This identifies the main cell type responsible for processing head direction signals, a core finding about circuit function.

fact: LR neurons have the largest excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP) amplitudes when anterior thalamic inputs target layer 1a, corresponding to the peak projection density of anterior dorsal anteroventral (ADAV) axons.
source_span: We found that LR neurons have the largest EPSP amplitude when the LED pulse is targeting layer 1a , corresponding with the peak projection density of ADAV axons and terminal arbors at this lamina.
selection_reasoning: This links anatomical input patterns to functional responses, explaining how LR neurons are tuned to thalamic inputs.

source_span: In contrast , the RS neuron showed much smaller EPSP amplitude with no significant variation in response across the layers.
selection_reasoning: This contrasts RS neurons with LR neurons, clarifying cell-type specificity in thalamic input processing.

fact: The laminar pattern of anterior thalamic inputs functionally aligns with the dendritic distribution of LR neurons but not RS neurons in the RSG.
source_span: This lamination of functional responses in the LR population precisely aligns with the lamination of ADAV axons and terminal arbors within these superficial layers.
selection_reasoning: This supports the conclusion that LR neurons are anatomically and functionally specialized for thalamic input.

source_span: This demonstrates that LR neurons are uniquely anatomically adapted to respond to incoming inputs from the anterior thalamus ... due to a precise overlap of their apical dendrites with the dense thalamic axons and terminals in the uppermost sublamina of L1 ( L1a ).
selection_reasoning: This explains the anatomical basis for LR neurons' selective responsiveness to thalamic inputs.

fact: Claustrum (CLA) and anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) provide major inputs to the RSG, with distinct laminar projection patterns different from anterior thalamic inputs.
source_span: Two other main sources of input to RSG are the claustrum ( CLA ) ... and anterior cingulate cortex ( ACC ) ... Both claustrocortical ( ClaC ) and ACC corticocortical ( CC ) projections have been anatomically shown to exhibit distinct laminar organization within its target cortical layers ...
selection_reasoning: This provides background on other important inputs to RSG relevant to the study's broader circuit context.

fact: RS neurons, but not LR neurons, anatomically overlap with claustral axons and terminals in superficial layers 1c, 2, and upper layer 5 of the RSG.
source_span: Dendritic lamination plots of LR and RS dendrites and projection density plots of CLA axons and terminal arbors show that RS , but not LR , apical dendrites anatomically overlap with CLA arbors in superficial layers 1 c and two and upper layer 5.
selection_reasoning: This identifies the cell type targeted by claustral inputs, a key finding about input specificity.

fact: RS neurons have significantly larger EPSP responses to claustral inputs compared to LR neurons when stimulated at layer 1/2, the area of strongest claustral projection density.
source_span: We found that RS neurons have significantly larger responses to CLA input compared to LR neurons when stimulated at layer 1/2 ... the area of the strongest superficial projection density of CLA arbors.

source_span: We found that RS neurons have the largest EPSP amplitude when the LED pulse is stimulating both layer 1c and 5sup ... In contrast , the complementary LR cell had no response to LED stimulation at any of the laminar locations.

fact: The functional lamination of claustral inputs in RS neurons aligns precisely with the lamination of claustral axons and terminal arbors in the RSG.
source_span: This lamination of functional responses in the RS cell precisely aligns with the lamination of ClaC axons and terminal arbors.
selection_reasoning: This confirms the anatomical-functional correspondence for claustral inputs to RS neurons.

fact: Regular-spiking (RS) neurons in retrosplenial granular cortex (RSG) receive stronger excitatory inputs from claustrum (CLA) afferents at layers 1c and 5 compared to layer 1a.
source_span: Population analysis showed that within the RS cell population, RS cells have significantly larger responses at L1/2 (p=0.00725) and L5sup (p=0.0301) compared to those at L1a (paired t-test; Figure 3G). source_span: In contrast, LR EPSP amplitudes across all layers were much lower in magnitude and did not differ from responses at L1a (p>0.05 for all; paired t-test; Figure 3G), indicating no significant lamination of functional responses to ClaC inputs in the LR population.

source_span: We found that DS afferents to layer 3 of RSG precisely overlap with LR basal and, to a lesser degree, proximal apical dendrites... LR neurons responded with significantly larger EPSPs compared to RS neurons when DS inputs were stimulated at the cell body in layer 3 (p=0.004).

source_span: Our high-resolution protocol and population analysis also confirmed that LR cells had significantly larger responses at layers 1/2 and 3 compared to L1a (L1/2 p=0.0132, L3 p=0.0135), suggesting the possibility of integration of synchronous anterior thalamic and dorsal subicular inputs by LR neurons.
