selection_reasoning: This fact supports the notion of parallel, distinct circuits formed by LR and RS neurons, central to the study's conclusions.

fact: Contralateral RSG inputs to RSG resemble CLA and ACC projections in laminar targeting and preferentially activate RS cells with minimal activation of LR cells.
source_span: Supplemental examination of contralateral RSG (cRSG) inputs to RSG showed lamination and resulting cell-type-specific targeting resembling that of projections from CLA and ACC... resulting in strong activation of RS cells, with almost no responses in LR cells.
selection_reasoning: This fact extends the anatomical and functional segregation of inputs, reinforcing the parallel circuit model.

fact: Similar laminar dichotomies between thalamic and claustral/corticocortical projections exist in other cortical regions such as the medial prefrontal cortex.
source_span: Importantly, laminar dichotomies similar to those seen here in RSG also exist between TC and ClaC/corticocortical projections to other cortical regions such as the medial prefrontal cortex.
selection_reasoning: This fact places the findings in a broader cortical context, suggesting generality and significance beyond RSG.

fact: Anterior thalamic inputs from ADAV to LR neurons in RSG exhibit unique and significant synaptic depression at 10 Hz stimulation, unlike DS inputs which show weak facilitation.
source_span: 10 Hz anterior thalamic inputs from ADAV to RSG LR neurons were uniquely and significantly depressing... In contrast, 10 Hz DS inputs to LR neurons were not depressing and exhibited weak facilitation.
selection_reasoning: This fact reveals a key functional difference in synaptic dynamics that may underlie distinct processing roles of these inputs.

fact: CLA and ACC inputs to RS neurons in RSG show weak synaptic facilitation at 10 Hz stimulation.
source_span: Both CLA and ACC inputs to RS cells were also weakly facilitating.
selection_reasoning: This fact complements the synaptic dynamics profile of inputs to RS neurons, important for understanding circuit function.

fact: Synaptic depression of anterior thalamic inputs to LR neurons is distinct from anterior thalamic inputs to superficial principal neurons in prefrontal cortex and anterior cingulate cortex.
source_span: Thus, the synaptic depression of anterior thalamic inputs to LR neurons is unique among the inputs examined here and also distinct from anterior thalamic inputs to superficial principal neurons in PFC and ACC.
selection_reasoning: This fact emphasizes the unique synaptic properties of ADAV inputs to LR neurons, highlighting specialized circuit function.

fact: Synaptic depression of anterior thalamic inputs to LR neurons increases with higher stimulation frequency, being stronger at 40 Hz than at 10 Hz.
source_span: 40 Hz inputs resulted in stronger depression than 10 Hz.
selection_reasoning: This fact provides insight into frequency-dependent synaptic dynamics relevant to physiological signaling.

fact: Computational modeling shows that synaptic depression of head direction (HD) inputs to LR neurons introduces an angular head speed signal, making LR neurons more responsive during faster head turns.
source_span: We found that the firing rate of the postsynaptic LR cell receiving HD input via depressing synapses was strongly correlated with angular head speed... Taken together, these results suggest that synaptic depression of HD ensemble inputs introduces an angular head speed signal into the LR population, producing neurons that are more responsive during faster head turns.
selection_reasoning: This fact links synaptic dynamics to a functional role in spatial orientation, a principal finding with translational relevance.

fact: Up to 60% of cells in the anterior thalamus are classical head direction cells, each with a unique preferred direction covering the full range of compass directions.
source_span: Up to 60% of cells in the anterior thalamus are classical head direction (HD) cells... The preferred directions of all cells in the HD ensemble span the full range of compass directions.
selection_reasoning: This background fact is necessary to understand the significance of HD inputs and their role in spatial processing.

fact: Synaptic depression of head direction (HD) ensemble inputs introduces an angular head speed signal into the low-rheobase (LR) neuron population in the retrosplenial granular cortex (RSG).
source_span: Taken together, these results suggest that synaptic depression of HD ensemble inputs introduces an angular head speed signal into the LR population, producing neurons that are more responsive during faster head turns, and potentially supporting the spatial orientation encoding functions attributed to the RSG.
selection_reasoning: This fact links synaptic mechanisms to the encoding of angular head speed, a core finding relevant to spatial orientation and the function of the RSG.

fact: Anterior thalamic head direction cells display anticipatory firing, becoming most active before the animal faces the cell’s preferred direction, with a mean anticipatory time interval (ATI) of 25–50 ms.
source_span: Anterior thalamic HD cells display anticipatory firing (Blair et al., 1997), a phenomenon where an HD cell becomes most active at a fixed time interval before the animal is facing that cell’s preferred direction... In anterior thalamus, the mean ATI has been reported as 25–50 ms (Taube, 2010).
selection_reasoning: This background fact defines anticipatory firing and ATI, which is central to understanding the study’s investigation of how ATI affects speed coding.

fact: Increasing the anticipatory time interval (ATI) of HD cells improves the timing and quality of angular head speed coding by LR neurons, reducing latency and enhancing tuning independent of lag.
source_span: Increasing ATI from 0 ms (no anticipation by the HD cell) to higher values... improved the lag between LR firing rate and angular head speed, with larger ATIs resulting in shorter latency between the head movement and LR coding of that angular head speed... larger ATIs also improved the angular head speed tuning of LR neurons independent of lag.
selection_reasoning: This is a principal finding showing how anticipatory firing enhances the neural encoding of head speed, a key mechanistic insight.

fact: Analytical modeling shows that synaptic depression of HD cell inputs onto LR cells results in angular speed coding, and anticipatory firing compensates for integration lag, enabling near-perfect speed coding.
source_span: Our analysis allowed us to mathematically derive that LR activity should encode head speed with depressing synapses from simplified HD cells... anticipatory firing compensates for the lag introduced by integration time, leading to a theoretical parameter regime for which postsynaptic speed coding can be essentially perfect.
selection_reasoning: This theoretical result supports and explains the simulation findings, strengthening the mechanistic understanding of speed coding.

fact: Postsynaptic LR neuron activity at lower rotational speeds is proportional to the square of head speed, explaining the parabolic shape of the speed-firing rate curve.
source_span: Our analysis showed that postsynaptic activity, at least at lower rotational speeds, is proportional to the square of head speed, thereby explaining the concave-up, parabolic shape of the speed-firing rate curve.
selection_reasoning: This fact explains a key characteristic of the neural response curve, linking firing rate to head speed quantitatively.

fact: Heterogeneity in the preferred head directions of presynaptic HD cells creates a tradeoff in LR neurons between encoding head direction and encoding head speed.
source_span: We found that single cell activity in the LR population could encode both head direction and head speed, but there was a clear tradeoff between the two types of information... This tradeoff between directional versus speed encoding was explained by the level of heterogeneity in the presynaptic preferred direction distribution.
selection_reasoning: This finding reveals how input diversity shapes the conjunctive coding properties of LR neurons, a key functional implication.

fact: LR neurons in the retrosplenial granular cortex are predicted to encode both head direction and rotational speed in vivo, with individual cells showing a tradeoff between these two types of information.
source_span: Overall, our results predict in vivo LR neuronal spike trains that are likely to correlate with both the head direction and rotational speed of an animal, with a tradeoff between direction versus speed coding seen across individual LR cells.
selection_reasoning: This summarizes the main translational implication of the study’s findings for neural coding in behaving animals.

fact: Low-rheobase (LR) cells are a unique, small, excitable pyramidal neuron type that defines the granular retrosplenial cortex (RSG).
source_span: The small, excitable LR cells are unique among pyramidal cells in RSG, and there is no evidence, to our knowledge, for such cells in any other cortical regions... Thus, LR cells are the defining morphological feature of RSG.
selection_reasoning: This background fact provides essential context about the cell type studied and its anatomical specificity.

fact: Low-rheobase (LR) neurons are a unique type of pyramidal cell found specifically in the granular retrosplenial cortex (RSG) and are not present in other cortical regions.
source_span: excitable LR cells are unique among pyramidal cells in RSG , and there is no evidence , to our knowledge , for such cells in any other cortical regions
selection_reasoning: This background fact defines the cell type central to the study and its unique anatomical location, which is critical for understanding the research focus.

fact: LR neurons have distinct electrophysiological properties, including low rheobase and lack of spike frequency adaptation, which are their defining computational features.
source_span: the low rheobase and lack of spike frequency adaptation of these neurons are their defining computational features
selection_reasoning: This fact explains the key physiological characteristics that distinguish LR neurons and motivate their study.

fact: LR neurons in the RSG play an integral role in processing anterior thalamic head direction inputs.
source_span: The distinct electrophysiological properties of LR neurons , specifically , play an integral role in the RSG’s unique capacity to process anterior thalamic head direction inputs
selection_reasoning: This fact links LR neurons to a key functional role relevant to spatial orientation, central to the study's main question.

fact: The dorsal subiculum transmits allocentric spatial information and projects predominantly to layer 3 of the RSG, targeting LR neurons.
source_span: The dorsal subiculum , which serves to transmit allocentric spatial information such as axis and boundary vector signals , also precisely targets LR neurons via projections predominantly to layer 3 of RSG
selection_reasoning: This fact provides important background on the spatial inputs LR neurons receive, relevant to their integrative function.

fact: LR neurons receive larger excitatory postsynaptic currents from dorsal subiculum inputs compared to layer 5 pyramidal neurons.
source_span: These inputs overlap with LR cell bodies , basal dendrites , and apical dendrites in L1b/c and evoke larger excitatory postsynaptic currents in superficial cells compared to layer 5 pyramidal neurons
selection_reasoning: This finding highlights the preferential targeting and stronger input to LR neurons, supporting their specialized role.

fact: Thalamocortical synapses onto LR neurons exhibit synaptic depression.
source_span: We have shown that thalamocortical synapses onto LR cells are depressing
selection_reasoning: This synaptic property is key to understanding how LR neurons process head direction signals.

fact: Synaptic depression at thalamocortical synapses enables LR neurons to compute angular head speed from head direction input, resulting in robust encoding of angular speed in LR firing rates.
source_span: Our modeling results demonstrate that such depressing synapses allow LR neurons to compute angular head speed from head direction input , leading to robust encoding of angular speed in the postsynaptic LR firing rate
selection_reasoning: This is a principal finding linking synaptic mechanisms to the computational function of LR neurons.

fact: Anticipatory firing of input head direction cells improves LR neurons' encoding of angular head speed by reducing time lag and strengthening correlation with head speed.
source_span: We also find that LR encoding of angular head speed is improved by the fact that input HD cells display anticipatory firing ... This improvement not only allows LR cells to encode current head speed with a shorter time lag , but also strengthens the correlation with head speed regardless of lag
selection_reasoning: This finding refines the understanding of how LR neurons achieve precise head speed encoding.

fact: Thalamocortical synapses onto LR neurons support conjunctive encoding of both head direction and angular head speed by individual LR cells.
source_span: we have shown that this thalamocortical synapse can support conjunctive encoding of both head direction and angular head speed by individual LR cells
selection_reasoning: This fact highlights the integrative coding capacity of LR neurons, a key conclusion.

fact: LR neurons are likely to show high firing rates and spike widths intermediate between regular-spiking and fast-spiking cells, predicting a distinct electrophysiological cluster in superficial RSG.
source_span: LR cells in superficial RSG are likely to show high firing rates and spike widths intermediate to the standard ‘broad/narrow’ criteria currently used to distinguish putative RS and FS cells
selection_reasoning: This prediction about LR neuron firing properties is important for future experimental validation and understanding their identity.

fact: LR neurons are the predominant spatial information-encoding pyramidal cell subtype within the RSG, showing significantly larger responses to thalamocortical input than layer 5 pyramidal neurons.
source_span: our results , reporting significantly larger responses to TC input by LR neurons , suggest LR cells are the predominant spatial information-encoding subtype within RSG
selection_reasoning: This key finding establishes LR neurons as the main functional cell type for spatial processing in RSG.

fact: The retrosplenial cortex integrates various types of directional and distance information, a function likely served by LR neurons in the RSG.
source_span: this integration of various types of directional and distance information is often stated as the key computational function of the retrosplenial cortex as a whole ... further highlighting the defining role that LR cells are likely to serve in the RSG
selection_reasoning: This fact situates LR neurons within the broader functional role of the retrosplenial cortex, emphasizing their significance.

fact: LR cells in superficial retrosplenial granular cortex (RSG) are predicted to have high firing rates and spike widths intermediate between regular-spiking (RS) and fast-spiking (FS) cells.
source_span: First , based on their intrinsic properties ( Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Brennan et al . , 2020 ) , LR cells in superficial RSG are likely to show high firing rates and spike widths intermediate to the standard ‘broad/narrow’ criteria currently used to distinguish putative RS and FS cells in most cortical recordings .
selection_reasoning: This background fact defines the physiological properties of LR cells, which is central to understanding their coding role and distinguishes them from other cell types.

fact: LR cell activity is expected to be correlated with angular head speed with a relatively small lag.
source_span: Second , we expect LR cell activity to be correlated with angular head speed with a relatively small lag ( Figures 8 and 9 ) .
selection_reasoning: This is a key predicted functional property of LR cells relevant to their role in encoding head movement information.

fact: The head velocity tuning curves of LR cells are predicted to be concave up and exhibit approximately quadratic scaling at low rotational speeds.
source_span: Third , we predict that the experimentally observed head velocity tuning curves will be concave up and exhibit approximately quadratic scaling at low rotational speeds , as our analytical work suggests ( Figure 8; Appendix ) .
selection_reasoning: This prediction about the shape of tuning curves is a principal finding related to how LR cells encode head velocity.

fact: A significant proportion of LR cells are predicted to show conjunctive encoding of both angular head speed and direction, with individual cells trading off between directional and speed encoding.
source_span: Fourth , we anticipate a significant proportion of LR cells will show conjunctive encoding , where both angular head speed and direction are encoded . A key aspect of this conjunctive encoding , as predicted by our simulations ( Figure 10 ) , is that individual cells will show a tradeoff between directional and speed encoding .
selection_reasoning: This conjunctive encoding is a central functional claim about LR cells' role in spatial orientation.

fact: LR cells likely provide comprehensive conjunctive speed and directional information to downstream targets, supporting spatial orientation computations within RSG.
source_span: As a population , this is likely to allow LR cells to comprehensively encode conjunctive speed and directional information and provide this information to downstream targets , helping with spatial orientation computations within RSG .
selection_reasoning: This fact highlights the significance of LR cells in spatial orientation processing.

fact: LR neurons do not synapse onto neighboring excitatory neurons within layers 2/3 or layer 5 regular-spiking cells in ipsilateral RSG.
source_span: LR neurons do not synapse onto neighboring excitatory neurons within layers 2/3 ( Brennan et al . , 2020 ) , and no ( 0/9 ) pairs tested in this study between LR and layer 5 RS cells exhibited connectivity ( data not shown ) .
selection_reasoning: This connectivity fact is important for understanding the circuit role and output targets of LR cells.

fact: LR neurons send their axons into the corpus callosum and likely target homotopic regions of contralateral RSG.
source_span: Instead , LR neurons send their axons into the corpus callosum and may likely target homotopic regions of contralateral RSG ( Brennan et al . , 2020; Kurotani et al . , 2013 ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact describes the main output pathway of LR cells, relevant to their functional role.

fact: Inputs from contralateral RSG preferentially and strongly target RS neurons, with almost no recruitment of LR neurons.
source_span: Our supplementary results ( Figure 6—figure supplement 1 ) show that inputs from contralateral RSG preferentially and strongly target RS neurons , with almost no recruitment of LR neurons .
selection_reasoning: This fact clarifies the directionality and specificity of interhemispheric connectivity involving LR and RS cells.

fact: LR neurons in one hemisphere receive unilateral inputs from directional cells in the anterior thalamus.
source_span: Thus , we propose the following hypotheses for LR downstream targets and possible function: LR neurons in one hemisphere receive unilateral inputs from directional cells in the anterior thalamus ( Figures 1 , 2 and 6 ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact links LR cells to thalamic head direction inputs, central to their proposed function.

fact: LR cells encode information about both the speed and direction of head rotations and transmit this information to RS cells in contralateral, but not ipsilateral, RSG.
source_span: These inputs are utilized to encode information about both the speed and direction of head rotations and are subsequently transmitted to RS cells in contralateral , but not ipsilateral , RSG ( Figure 6—figure supplement 1 ) .
selection_reasoning: This is a principal functional claim about LR cells' role in interhemispheric communication of spatial information.

fact: LR cells may serve to perform a hemispheric switch of rotational speed and direction information.
source_span: Thus , LR cells may serve to perform a hemispheric switch of rotational speed and direction information .
selection_reasoning: This is a key implication of the LR cell circuit function.

fact: RS cells may use inputs from contralateral LR cells to compare actual head speed and direction signals with motor efference signals, sharpening spatial orientation coding in RSG.
source_span: Given the known bidirectional connectivity between secondary motor cortex and RSG ( Yamawaki et al . , 2016a ) , RS cells may be able to utilize inputs from contralateral LR cells to perform comparisons of the actual head speed and direction signal with motor efference signals , helping to sharpen the code for spatial orientation in the RSG .
selection_reasoning: This fact links LR cell outputs to a broader sensorimotor integration function relevant to spatial orientation.

fact: Projections from the claustrum and anterior cingulate cortex avoid laminar overlap with LR apical dendrites and instead target RS apical and basal dendrites in lower layers.
source_span: In contrast to thalamic and DS inputs to RSG , projections from both the claustrum and anterior cingulate cortex avoid laminar overlap with LR apical dendrites , instead projecting to the lower divisions of L1/2 and L5 to target RS apical and basal dendrites ( Figures 3 and 4 , and 6 ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact distinguishes the input sources and laminar targeting of LR versus RS cells, relevant to their functional segregation.

fact: The claustrum and anterior cingulate cortex are implicated in cognitive and mnemonic functions but also exhibit some degree of spatial information processing.
source_span: Both the CLA and ACC are heavily implicated in a range of non-spatial behaviors often described as being ‘cognitive’ or ‘mnemonic’ in function ( Botvinick , 2007; Brown and Braver , 2005; Carter et al , 1998; Devinsky et al , 1995; Kim et al , 2016; Mohanty et al , 2007; Smith et al , 2012; Smythies et al , 2012; Stevens et al , 2011 ) , but there is also evidence that these regions exhibit some degree of spatial information processing ( Guterstam et al , 2015; Jankowski and O'Mara , 2015; Sutherland et al , 1988; Whishaw et al , 2001 ) .
selection_reasoning: This background fact contextualizes the functional roles of CLA and ACC inputs to RS cells.

fact: The retrosplenial cortex (RSC) plays a key role in contextual fear conditioning by integrating spatial and non-spatial information.
source_span: This convergence of disparate signals onto RS cells could then serve to support functions that require both spatial and non-spatial integration, such as contextual fear conditioning, a key function attributed to the RSC (de Sousa et al., 2019; Keene and Bucci, 2008a; Keene and Bucci, 2008b; Kwapis et al., 2015; Yamawaki et al., 2019a).
selection_reasoning: This fact provides important background and significance about the functional role of the retrosplenial cortex relevant to the study.

fact: Selective ablation of retrosplenial RS cells near the boundary and within upper layer 5 causes contextual fear amnesia, indicating these cells are involved in fear-related functions of the retrosplenial cortex.
source_span: Indeed, a recent study reported that selective ablation of putative retrosplenial RS cells located near the boundary and within upper layer 5 resulted in contextual fear amnesia (Sigwald et al., 2020), indicating that these cells are involved in the fear-related functions of the retrosplenial cortex (Lukoyanov and Lukoyanova, 2006; Yamawaki et al., 2019a; Yamawaki et al., 2019b).
selection_reasoning: This finding highlights a key functional role of a specific retrosplenial neuron subtype, supporting the study's focus on these cells.

fact: Claustrum (CLA) and anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) inputs preferentially target layer 3 retrosplenial RS neurons and are implicated in fear-associated behaviors.
source_span: Both the CLA (Cho et al., 2017; Ipser et al., 2013; Vakolyuk et al., 1980; Vetere et al., 2017; Zingg et al., 2018) and ACC (Frankland et al., 2004; Han et al., 2003; Steenland et al., 2012) have been heavily implicated in fear-associated behaviors, suggesting again that CLA and ACC inputs to L3 RS cells help to support the role of these neurons in contextual fear conditioning.
selection_reasoning: This fact links specific inputs to retrosplenial neurons with fear behavior, a central theme of the study.

fact: Retrosplenial LR neurons receive directional and spatial inputs from the anterior thalamus and dorsal subiculum.
source_span: LR neurons receive directional and spatial inputs from the anterior thalamus and dorsal subiculum.
selection_reasoning: This is a principal finding about the input specificity to retrosplenial neuron subtypes, central to the study's main question.

fact: Thalamic inputs to LR neurons exhibit synaptic dynamics that can produce rate coding of angular head speed.
source_span: The synaptic dynamics of thalamic inputs to LR cells can give rise to rate coding of angular head speed in LR cells.
selection_reasoning: This fact describes a key mechanism discovered in the study linking synaptic properties to neural coding.

fact: Neighboring retrosplenial RS neurons respond weakly to directional inputs from anterior thalamus and dorsal subiculum because their dendrites avoid laminar overlap with these afferents.
source_span: In contrast, neighboring RS neurons in RSG respond very weakly to these directional inputs, as their apical and basal dendrites distinctly avoid laminar overlap with anterior thalamic and subicular afferents.
selection_reasoning: This finding explains the differential input integration by retrosplenial neuron subtypes, a core result.

fact: Retrosplenial RS neurons respond instead to claustrocortical and anterior cingulate inputs.
source_span: Instead, RS neurons respond to claustrocortical and anterior cingulate inputs.
selection_reasoning: This fact complements the previous one by specifying the alternative inputs to RS neurons, important for understanding circuit organization.

fact: Feedforward inhibition regulates cortical signaling in retrosplenial circuits by modulating responses to thalamic and claustral inputs.
source_span: Matrix TC inputs evoke feedforward inhibition to regulate cortical signaling through both disinhibition (Anastasiades et al., 2021; Delevich et al., 2015) and the disynaptic inhibition of pyramidal neurons (Cruikshank et al., 2012; Yamawaki et al., 2019a; Yamawaki et al., 2019b). Similarly, ClaC inputs invoke feedforward inhibition in several cortical regions, particularly through recruitment of neuropeptide Y (NPY) and, to a lesser degree, FS cells (Jackson et al., 2018).
selection_reasoning: This fact highlights an important regulatory mechanism in the studied circuits, relevant to understanding information processing.

fact: Long-range inhibitory signals from hippocampal CA1 target apical dendrites in retrosplenial layer 1a and converge with excitatory anterior thalamic inputs to regulate retrosplenial circuits.
source_span: Long-range inhibitory signals from CA1 of the hippocampus also target apical dendrites in retrosplenial layer 1a, converging with excitatory anterior thalamic inputs, to precisely regulate these TC inputs and establish a hippocampo-thalamo-retrosplenial network (Yamawaki et al., 2019b).
selection_reasoning: This fact describes a key circuit interaction relevant to retrosplenial information processing.

fact: The study used a mouse model circuit consisting of retrosplenial LR cells receiving input from thalamic head direction cells with synapses exhibiting short-term depression.
source_span: Our model circuit consists of an RSG LR cell receiving input from an ensemble of N thalamic HD cells, via synapses exhibiting short-term depression.
selection_reasoning: This fact summarizes a key methodological approach used to investigate synaptic and coding properties.

fact: Thalamic head direction cells exhibit an anticipatory time interval (ATI), firing before the animal's heading reaches the cell's preferred direction.
source_span: Thalamic HD cells exhibit an anticipatory time interval, or ATI: for each cell, there exists some constant duration Ams such that the cell tends to spike Ams prior to when the animal’s heading equals the preferred direction of the cell.
selection_reasoning: This fact defines an important property of the input neurons relevant to the study's modeling and interpretation.

fact: Head direction (HD) cell preferred angles shift in anticipation of angular head velocity, effectively transforming the perceived heading trajectory.
source_span: The ATI is defined via the property that when angular head velocity equals ω , the PA of this cell shifts from θ to θ-ωA . Equivalently , we can think of HD cell PAs as static and instead say anticipatory firing effectively transforms the heading trajectory itself: if θTt describes the true angular trajectory , the effective trajectory experienced by our chosen HD cell is:θA ( t ) =θT ( t ) +A⋅θT˙ ( t )
selection_reasoning: This fact explains the core concept of anticipatory firing in HD cells, which is central to the study's background and modeling approach.

fact: In vivo mouse head tracking recordings were used to simulate angular head trajectories for studying HD cell activity.
source_span: To simulate the angular trajectory θTt , we employ in vivo mouse head tracking recordings from the data set CRCNS-th1 ( Peyrache et al . , 2015 ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact describes the key data source and biological system used to model HD cell responses.

fact: The Tsodyks-Markram (TM) model of short-term synaptic plasticity was used to characterize synaptic dynamics at HD cell synapses.
source_span: In the Tsodyks-Markram ( TM ) model ( Tsodyks et al . , 1998 ) of short-term synaptic plasticity , each synapse has a finite pool from which it releases vesicles into the cleft upon arrival of a presynaptic spike .
selection_reasoning: This fact highlights the main synaptic plasticity model applied to understand synaptic behavior in the study.

fact: Synaptic dynamics can be dominated by depression or facilitation depending on the relative timescales of recovery and decay in the TM model.
source_span: In the regime of τd≫τf , depression dominates the synaptic dynamics; conversely , in the regime of τf≫τd , facilitation dominates .
selection_reasoning: This fact explains a key mechanistic insight about synaptic behavior relevant to interpreting simulation results.

fact: Parameters for the TM model were fitted to experimental EPSP data from thalamocortical stimulation of retrosplenial granular (RSG) layer (LR) cells, resulting in moderately depressing synaptic dynamics.
source_span: We obtained this parameter set by fitting the TM model response to recorded EPSP amplitudes evoked via thalamocortical stimulation of RSG LR cells with a 10 Hz pulse train ... The resultant TM dynamics were moderately depressing , in accordance with the experimental results .
selection_reasoning: This fact links the model parameters to experimental data, supporting the biological relevance of the simulations.

fact: The postsynaptic LR cell was modeled using a morphologically detailed Hodgkin-Huxley conductance-based model including fast sodium, delayed rectifier potassium, and Kv1.1-mediated slow potassium currents.
source_span: We model the postsynaptic LR cell using the morphologically detailed model originally presented in Brennan et al . , 2020 . This model , implemented in NEURON ... consists of Hodgkin-Huxley conductances representing a fast sodium current , a delayed rectifier potassium current , and a Kv1 . 1-mediated slow potassium current .
selection_reasoning: This fact describes the principal postsynaptic neuron model used to study synaptic input integration.

fact: Each postsynaptic LR cell receives input from multiple presynaptic HD cells, each with a unique preferred angle (PA).
source_span: Each postsynaptic cell receives input from N presynaptic HD cells , each of which has a unique PA .
selection_reasoning: This fact is central to the network input structure and the study of how HD cell populations influence postsynaptic responses.

fact: The distribution of HD cell preferred angles can be uniform or nonuniform, with nonuniform distributions modeled using Brownian bridge processes to ensure circular continuity.
source_span: When studying postsynaptic speed coding , we initially drew the PA of each HD cell uniformly at random from 0 , 2π . Later on , we examined the effect of introducing nonuniform PA distributions ... modeled the PA distribution probability densities randomly as resulting from Brownian bridge processes ( to ensure 2π periodicity of the density ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact explains how variability in HD cell tuning was incorporated, which affects postsynaptic coding.

fact: Postsynaptic activity was analyzed for its relationship to head turning speed using time-lagged Pearson correlation and mutual information measures.
source_span: To quantify the extent to which postsynaptic activity reflects head turning speed , we utilized two similarity measures M: Pearson correlation and mutual information . In fact , we used the time-lagged counterparts of these measures ...
selection_reasoning: This fact describes the key analytical approach to assess how well postsynaptic firing encodes head movement speed.

fact: Petal number is invariant in Arabidopsis thaliana flowers but varies in the closely related species Cardamine hirsuta.
source_span: Petal number, for example, is invariant in Arabidopsis thaliana flowers. However, petal number varies in the closely related species Cardamine hirsuta, and the genetic basis for this difference between species is unknown.
selection_reasoning: This fact establishes the key biological difference motivating the study and frames the main research question.

fact: Divergence in the floral regulator APETALA1 (AP1) explains the species-specific difference in petal number robustness between Arabidopsis thaliana and Cardamine hirsuta.
source_span: Here we show that divergence in the pleiotropic floral regulator APETALA1 (AP1) can account for the species-specific difference in petal number robustness.
selection_reasoning: This is the principal finding linking a specific gene to the difference in petal number robustness, central to the study's conclusion.

fact: Arabidopsis thaliana AP1 confers robustness in petal number by masking the effects of quantitative trait loci controlling petal number in Cardamine hirsuta.
source_span: This large effect of AP1 is explained by epistatic interactions: A. thaliana AP1 confers robustness by masking the phenotypic expression of quantitative trait loci controlling petal number in C. hirsuta.
selection_reasoning: This fact explains the mechanism by which AP1 affects petal number robustness, a key insight into gene interaction.

fact: Cardamine hirsuta AP1 fails to complement the robustness function of Arabidopsis thaliana AP1, resulting in variable petal number.
source_span: We show that C. hirsuta AP1 fails to complement this function of A. thaliana AP1, conferring variable petal number, and that upstream regulatory regions of AP1 contribute to this divergence.
selection_reasoning: This fact highlights the functional divergence of AP1 between species, explaining the phenotypic difference.

fact: Upstream regulatory regions of AP1 contribute to the divergence in petal number robustness between Arabidopsis thaliana and Cardamine hirsuta.
source_span: …and that upstream regulatory regions of AP1 contribute to this divergence.
selection_reasoning: This identifies a genetic mechanism underlying the functional differences in AP1, important for understanding evolutionary changes.

fact: Variable petal number is maintained in Cardamine hirsuta despite sufficient genetic variation in natural populations to produce four-petalled flowers.
source_span: Moreover, variable petal number is maintained in C. hirsuta despite sufficient standing genetic variation in natural accessions to produce plants with four-petalled flowers.
selection_reasoning: This fact shows that genetic variation alone does not explain robustness, emphasizing the role of AP1 divergence.

fact: Petal number is a robust trait in flowering plants, usually invariant within species and higher taxonomic orders, likely due to stabilizing selection.
source_span: Petal number is a robust trait in flowering plants and usually invariant within species and even higher taxonomic orders… suggesting that this trait was canalized during angiosperm evolution to produce a stable phenotype in the face of genetic and environmental perturbation.
selection_reasoning: This background fact explains why petal number robustness is biologically important and evolutionarily conserved.

fact: A stable number of petals helps ensure reliable display of reproductive organs and consistent cues for pollinators.
source_span: Petals are usually required to open the flower and to help attract pollinators… therefore a stable number of petals could ensure a reliable display of the reproductive organs and a reproducible cue for pollinators.
selection_reasoning: This fact provides biological significance for why petal number robustness matters for plant reproduction.

fact: Petal number variation in Cardamine hirsuta is influenced by both environmental factors such as season and temperature, and natural genetic variation.
source_span: This phenotype varies in response to both environmental and genetic perturbation. C. hirsuta flowers show seasonal variation in petal number… Seasonal cues, such as day length, winter cold, and particularly ambient temperature, all influence the number of petals produced in C. hirsuta flowers… Furthermore, petal number is strongly influenced by natural genetic variation in C. hirsuta.
selection_reasoning: This fact contextualizes the complexity of petal number variation within C. hirsuta, relevant to understanding the trait's regulation.

fact: Quantitative trait loci (QTL) of small to moderate effect contribute to petal number variation in Cardamine hirsuta natural populations.
source_span: A polygenic architecture of small to moderate effect quantitative trait loci (QTL), that shift the trait in both directions, contribute to petal number variation in C. hirsuta.

source_span: Alleles of large effect and low pleiotropy were identified in genetic screens for four-petalled mutants in C. hirsuta, but were not detected by QTL analysis in natural accessions.

fact: Petal number is a robust phenotype in Arabidopsis thaliana, with flowers consistently producing four petals across genetically diverse accessions.
source_span: The flowers of A . thaliana and other Brassicaceae species are readily distinguished by their four petals . This phenotype is robust to natural genetic variation; for example , flowers from genetically diverse A . thaliana accessions consistently produce four petals
selection_reasoning: This background fact establishes the baseline robustness of petal number in A. thaliana, which is central to the study's comparison with C. hirsuta.

fact: Cardamine hirsuta shows variable petal number, ranging from zero to four petals, distinguishing it from Arabidopsis thaliana.
source_span: C . hirsuta lacks this robustness and shows variation in petal number . For example , we found similar frequencies of each petal number between zero and four in flowers from 39 C . hirsuta accessions sampled from across the species range
selection_reasoning: This fact defines the main biological difference under investigation and motivates the study of petal number variation.

fact: The evolutionary transition from a robust four-petal phenotype in A. thaliana to variable petal number in C. hirsuta is associated with divergence in the floral regulator gene AP1.
source_span: In this study , we investigate the evolutionary transition from a robust phenotype of four petals , typified by A . thaliana , to a variable petal number in C . hirsuta . We show that divergence in the pleiotropic floral regulator AP1 can account for the difference in petal number robustness between species
selection_reasoning: This is a principal finding linking a specific gene to the phenotypic difference, central to the study's main claim.

fact: AP1 from Arabidopsis thaliana masks the phenotypic expression of all petal number quantitative trait loci (QTL) in Cardamine hirsuta, conferring robustness to petal number.
source_span: This large effect of AP1 is explained by epistatic interactions: A . thaliana AP1 masks the phenotypic expression of all petal number QTL in C . hirsuta and , in this way , confers robustness
selection_reasoning: This mechanistic insight explains how robustness is genetically controlled, a key scientific claim.

fact: Cardamine hirsuta AP1 fails to complement the petal number robustness function of Arabidopsis thaliana AP1, resulting in variable petal number.
source_span: We show that C . hirsuta AP1 fails to complement this function of A . thaliana AP1 , conferring variable petal number
selection_reasoning: This fact supports the functional divergence of AP1 between species, critical to understanding the genetic basis of variation.

fact: Differences in upstream regulatory regions of AP1 contribute to the divergence in petal number robustness between Arabidopsis thaliana and Cardamine hirsuta.

fact: Petal primordia often fail to initiate in the second whorl of Cardamine hirsuta flowers at early developmental stages, unlike in Arabidopsis thaliana where petal primordia are consistently observed.

fact: Auxin activity maxima mark sites of petal initiation in Arabidopsis thaliana but often fail to form or are aberrantly located in Cardamine hirsuta floral meristems.
source_span: At sites of petal initiation in A . thaliana , auxin activity maxima formed in 2 – 3 epidermal cells on the floral meristem flank prior to growth of these cells . However , in C . hirsuta , auxin activity maxima often failed to form on the floral meristem , and instead were either absent or aberrantly located in the first whorl between sepals
selection_reasoning: This fact provides a key developmental mechanism difference underlying petal number variation.

fact: The ptl mutant in Arabidopsis thaliana mimics the variable petal number phenotype of Cardamine hirsuta and shows a similar auxin activity distribution during petal initiation.

fact: Differences in PTL function are unlikely to account for the variation in petal number between Cardamine hirsuta and Arabidopsis thaliana.

fact: In yeast, mitophagy primarily functions to adapt to metabolic changes rather than in protein quality control, and there is little evidence that mitophagy is ubiquitin-dependent in yeast.
source_span: In yeast , however , mitophagy appears to function primarily to adapt to metabolic changes , rather than in protein QC . Furthermore , there is little evidence indicating that mitophagy is ubiquitin-dependent , in accordance with the absence of obvious yeast orthologues of Parkin or PINK1 .
selection_reasoning: This clarifies why alternative mitochondrial protein quality control pathways, such as mitochondria-associated degradation, are important in yeast.

fact: The mitochondrial outer membrane is accessible to cytosolic proteasomes, enabling degradation of misfolded proteins via the ubiquitin-proteasome system.
source_span: While there is no evidence for proteasomes inside mitochondria , the mitochondrial outer membrane ( MOM ) is fully accessible to cytosolic proteasomes .
selection_reasoning: This fact supports the mechanistic basis for degradation of MOM proteins by the ubiquitin-proteasome system.

fact: The regulated recognition and ubiquitination of the mitofusin Fzo1 by the SCFMdm30 E3 ligase and its subsequent proteasomal degradation are integral to mitochondrial outer membrane (MOM) fusion.
source_span: The regulated recognition and ubiquitination of this mitofusin by SCFMdm30 ( Skp1-Cullin-F-box E3 with F-box protein Mdm30 ) and its subsequent proteasomal degradation are integral to the process of MOM fusion ( Cohen et al . , 2011; Cohen et al . , 2008; Escobar-Henriques et al . , 2006 ) .
selection_reasoning: This background fact explains a key known mechanism of MOM protein regulation relevant to the study of mitochondrial protein quality control.

fact: The AAA-ATPase Msp1 is required for extraction of mislocalized tail-anchored proteins from the mitochondrial outer membrane prior to their degradation by ER-associated degradation (ERAD) machinery.
source_span: The degradation of tail-anchored proteins mislocalized to the MOM uniquely requires the AAA-ATPase Msp1 for extraction from the MOM prior to transfer to the ER where they are degraded by ERAD machinery ( Matsumoto et al . , 2019; Okreglak and Walter , 2014; Wohlever et al . , 2017 ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact provides important context about mitochondrial protein quality control pathways and highlights a known mechanism distinct from the pathway studied here.

fact: A universal mitochondrial-associated degradation (MAD) pathway for mitochondrial outer membrane proteins has not been described, and many steps in substrate degradation remain unexamined.
source_span: Thus , a universal MAD pathway for MOM proteins has not been described and many steps in substrate degradation remain unexamined .
selection_reasoning: This motivates the study by identifying a key knowledge gap in mitochondrial protein quality control.

fact: Temperature-sensitive peripheral mitochondrial outer membrane proteins sam35-2HAts and sen2-1HAts were established as quality control substrates to study mitochondrial degradation.
source_span: In this study , we establish temperature-sensitive ( ts- ) peripheral MOM proteins ( sam35-2HAts and sen2-1HAts ) as QC substrates .

fact: The temperature-sensitive nature of sam35-2HAts and sen2-1HAts, combined with their tight association with the mitochondrial outer membrane, enables study of their mitochondrial degradation without concerns of mislocalization.
source_span: The ts- nature of these substrates , coupled with their tight association with the MOM , enabled study of their mitochondrial degradation without concerns of mislocalization to the cytosol or elsewhere .
selection_reasoning: This explains why these substrates are suitable models for studying mitochondrial protein degradation.

fact: Proteasomal degradation of these mitochondrial-associated degradation (MAD) quality control substrates occurs at the mitochondrial outer membrane and requires specific cytosolic and mitochondrial ubiquitin-proteasome system components conserved in higher eukaryotes.
source_span: The proteasomal degradation of these MAD QC substrates occurs at the MOM and requires specific cytosolic and mitochondrial UPS components , most of which are conserved in higher eukaryotes .
selection_reasoning: This is a principal finding linking proteasomal degradation and specific UPS components to mitochondrial protein quality control.

Combined with factors like breeding habitat availability , vector control , humidity , human and reservoir host density , host immune status , and mosquito exposure , relative R0 can be used to predict disease incidence . In this approach , only the relative thermal response of each trait influences R0 , which is desirable since traits can differ substantially due to other factors and in laboratory versus field settings ( particularly mosquito survival: Clements and Paterson , 1981 ) . Relative R0 does not provide a threshold for sustained disease transmission ( i . e . where absolute R0 = 1 ) , since this threshold is not controlled solely by temperature . Instead , relative R0 preserves the temperature-dependence of R0 to provide three key temperature values: upper and lower thermal limits where transmission is possible ( R0 >0; a conservative threshold where transmission is not excluded by high or low temperatures ) and the temperature that maximizes R0 .

source_span: there is some evidence for high temperatures constraining RRV transmission and vector populations: outbreaks were less likely with more days above 35°C in part of Queensland ( Gatton et al . , 2005 ) and populations of Cx . annulirostris peaked at 25°C and declined above 32°C in Victoria ( Dhileepan , 1996 ) .

fact: Breeding habitat availability, influenced by rainfall, river flow, and tidal patterns, drives mosquito abundance and RRV disease incidence.
source_span: Breeding habitat availability also drives mosquito abundance and mosquito-borne disease . Local rainfall or river flow have been linked to the abundance of RRV vector species ( Barton et al . , 2004; Tall et al . , 2014; Jacups et al . , 2015 ) and RRV disease cases ( Tong and Hu , 2001; Tong et al . , 2002a; Hu et al . , 2004; Kelly-Hope et al . , 2004b; Tong et al . , 2004; Gatton et al . , 2005; Jacups et al . , 2008b; Bi et al . , 2009; Williams et al . , 2009; Werner et al . , 2012 ) , as have high tides in coastal areas with saltmarsh mosquitoes , Ae . vigilax and Ae . camptorhynchus ( Tong and Hu , 2002b; Tong et al . , 2004; Jacups et al . , 2008b; Kokkinn et al . , 2009 ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact identifies key environmental drivers of vector populations and disease, important for understanding transmission dynamics.

fact: Considering thermal constraints on mosquito abundance is critical because breeding habitat can only impact vector populations when temperatures are suitable.
source_span: Since breeding habitat can only impact vector populations when temperatures do not exclude them , it is critical to consider thermal constraints on mosquito abundance , even when breeding habitat is considered a stronger driver .
selection_reasoning: This fact highlights the interaction between temperature and habitat, important for accurate transmission modeling.

fact: Many mechanistic temperature-dependent models of vector-borne disease transmission do not include thermal effects on vector density, which can critically impact model results near thermal limits.
source_span: Nonetheless , many mechanistic , temperature-dependent models of vector-borne disease transmission do not include thermal effects on vector density ( Martens et al . , 1997; Craig et al . , 1999; Paull et al . , 2017; Caminade et al . , 2017; Hamlet et al . , 2018 ) . Our results demonstrate that the decision to exclude these relationships can have a critical impact on model results , especially near thermal limits .
selection_reasoning: This fact underscores a methodological gap and the significance of including vector density effects in models.

fact: Future validation of the relative R0 model should incorporate fine-scale temperature variation, breeding habitat drivers, and reservoir host dynamics to better predict RRV transmission and human cases.
source_span: First , the relative R0 model needs to be more rigorously validated using time series of cases to determine the importance of temperature at finer spatiotemporal scales . These analyses should incorporate daily , seasonal , and spatial temperature variation , including aquatic larval habitat and adult microhabitat temperatures ( Paaijmans et al . , 2010; Cator et al . , 2013; Carrington et al . , 2013; Thomas et al . , 2018 ) . They should also integrate species-specific drivers of breeding habitat availability , like rainfall and tidal patterns , infrastructure ( e . g . drainage ) , and human activities ( e . g . deliberate and accidental water storage ) . Second , translating environmental suitability for transmission into human cases also depends on disease dynamics in reservoir host populations and their impact on immunity .
selection_reasoning: This fact outlines key future research directions to improve model accuracy and disease prediction.

source_span: For instance , in Western Australia heavy summer rains can fail to initiate epidemics when low rainfall in the preceding winter depresses recruitment of susceptible juvenile kangaroos ( Mackenzie et al . , 2000 ) . By contrast , large outbreaks occur in southeastern Australia when high rainfall follows a dry year , presumably from higher transmission within relatively unexposed reservoir populations ( Woodruff et al . , 2002 ) .

fact: The full R0 model assumes temperature drives mosquito density and includes vector life history trait thermal responses.
source_span: The ‘full R0 model’ ( Equation 1 ) assumes temperature drives mosquito density and includes vector life history trait thermal responses ( Parham and Michael , 2009; Mordecai et al . , 2013; Mordecai et al . , 2017 ) .
selection_reasoning: This describes a key methodological approach used to model transmission.

fact: The constant M model assumes mosquito density does not depend on temperature.
source_span: The ‘constant M model’ ( Equation 2 ) assumes mosquito density ( M ) does not depend on temperature ( Dietz , 1993 ) .
selection_reasoning: This contrasts with the full model and is relevant for understanding modeling assumptions.

fact: The study used the next-generation matrix method to calculate R0 to be consistent with previous work on mosquito-borne diseases.
source_span: We use the version derived from the next-generation matrix method ( Dietz , 1993 ) in order to be consistent with our previous work in other mosquito-borne disease systems ( Mordecai et al . , 2013; Mordecai et al . , 2017; Johnson et al . , 2015 ) .
selection_reasoning: This clarifies the modeling framework and ensures methodological consistency.

fact: Mosquito life history traits such as biting rate, vector competence, adult mortality rate, parasite development rate, fecundity, egg-to-adult survival, and development rate depend on temperature and influence Ross River virus transmission.
source_span: In both equations , ( T ) indicates that a parameter depends on temperature , a is mosquito biting rate , bc is vector competence ( proportion of mosquitoes becoming infectious post-exposure ) , µ is adult mosquito mortality rate ( adult lifespan , lf = 1/µ ) , PDR is parasite development rate ( PDR = 1/EIP , the extrinsic incubation period ) , N is human density , and r is the recovery rate at which humans become immune ( all rates are measured in days−1 ) . The latter two terms do not depend on temperature . In the full R0 model , mosquito density ( M ) depends on fecundity ( EFD , eggs per female per day ) , proportion surviving from egg-to-adulthood ( pEA ) , and mosquito development rate ( MDR ) , divided by the square of adult mortality rate ( µ ) ( Parham and Michael , 2009 ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact summarizes the biological parameters central to the transmission model.

fact: Thermal responses of mosquito traits were fit using Bayesian inference with Brière or quadratic functions to capture asymmetrical or symmetrical temperature effects.
source_span: We fit thermal responses of each trait using Bayesian inference with the ‘r2jags’ package ( Plummer , 2003; Su and Yajima , 2009 ) in R ( R Core Team , 2017 ) . Traits with asymmetrical thermal responses were fit as Brière functions: qT ( T–Tmin ) ( Tmax–T ) 1/2 ( Briere et al . , 1999 ) . Traits with symmetrical thermal responses were fit as quadratic functions: -q ( T–Tmin ) ( T–Tmax ) .
selection_reasoning: This describes the key methodological approach to modeling temperature-dependent traits.

fact: Priors for thermal response parameters were informed by data from other mosquito species to improve fit accuracy and uncertainty representation.
source_span: For priors we used gamma distributions with hyperparameters derived from thermal responses fit to data from other mosquito species ( Figure 2—source data 2 ) ( Davis , 1932; Jalil , 1972; McLean et al . , 1974; Watts et al . , 1987; Rueda et al . , 1990; Focks et al . , 1993; Joshi , 1996; Teng and Apperson , 2000; Tun-Lin et al . , 2000; Alto and Juliano , 2001; Briegel and Timmermann , 2001; Kamimura et al . , 2002; Calado and Navarro-Silva , 2002; Focks and Barrera , 2006; Wiwatanaratanabutr and Kittayapong , 2006; Lardeux et al . , 2008; Delatte et al . , 2009; Beserra et al . , 2009; Yang et al . , 2009; Westbrook et al . , 2010; Muturi et al . , 2011; Carrington et al . , 2013; Tjaden et al . , 2013; Eisen et al . , 2014; Xiao et al . , 2014; Ezeakacha , 2015; Morin et al . , 2015 ) . These priors allowed us to more accurately represent the fit and uncertainty .
selection_reasoning: This fact explains how the modeling approach was strengthened by leveraging existing data.

fact: Biting rate and parasite development rate traits decline at high temperatures, approaching zero near 40°C.
source_span: data from other mosquito species ( Mordecai et al . , 2013; Mordecai et al . , 2017 ) and principles of thermal biology ( Dell et al . , 2011 ) imply these traits must decline at high temperatures . Thus , for those traits we included an artificial data point where the trait value approached zero at a very high temperature ( 40°C ) , allowing us to fit the Brière function .
selection_reasoning: This fact is central to modeling temperature effects on transmission and constraining the upper thermal limit of R0.

fact: Bayesian inference was used to estimate posterior distributions of trait thermal responses and R0, with medians reported to reduce sensitivity to outliers.
source_span: Bayesian inference produces estimated posterior distributions rather than a single estimated value . Because these distributions can be non-normal and asymmetric , we report and apply medians rather than means , since medians are less sensitive to outlying values in extended tails .
selection_reasoning: Describes the key statistical approach used to model uncertainty in trait and transmission estimates.

fact: Sensitivity and uncertainty analyses were conducted to determine how individual mosquito traits influence the temperature-dependent transmission potential (R0).
source_span: We conducted sensitivity and uncertainty analyses of the full R0 model ( Equation 1 ) to understand how trait thermal responses shape the thermal response of R0 . We examined the sensitivity of R0 two ways . First , we evaluated the impact of each trait by setting it constant while allowing all other traits to vary with temperature . Second , we calculated the partial derivative of R0 with respect to each trait across temperature .
selection_reasoning: This fact highlights the main analytical approach to identify which traits most affect transmission across temperatures.

fact: Monthly mean temperatures from seven Australian cities spanning tropical to temperate climates were used to calculate temperature-dependent R0 values for Ross River virus transmission.
source_span: We took monthly mean temperatures from WorldClim for seven cities spanning a latitudinal and temperature gradient ( from tropical North to temperate South: Darwin , Cairns , Brisbane , Perth , Sydney , Melbourne , and Hobart ) and calculated the posterior median R0 ( T ) for each month at each location .
selection_reasoning: This fact describes the geographic and climatic scope of the transmission modeling.

fact: A population-weighted average R0 was calculated for Australia's fifteen most populous urban areas and compared to nationally aggregated Ross River virus case data from 1992 to 2013.
source_span: We used 2016 estimates for the fifteen most populous urban areas , which together contain 76 . 6% of Australia’s population . We calculated R0 ( T ) for each location and estimated a population-weighted average . We compared this country-scale estimate of R0 ( T ) with data on mean monthly human cases of RRV nationwide from 1992 to 2013 obtained from the National Notifiable Diseases Surveillance System .
selection_reasoning: This fact links modeled transmission potential to observed human disease incidence at a national scale.

fact: There is an estimated two-month time lag between temperature-driven transmission potential (R0) and reported human Ross River virus cases due to mosquito and human incubation periods and reporting delays.
source_span: We hypothesize a two-month time lag between R0 ( T ) and RRV disease cases . Empirical work on dengue vectors in Ecuador identified a six-week time lag between temperature and mosquito oviposition . Subsequent mosquito development and incubation periods in mosquitoes and humans likely add another 2–4 week lag before cases appear .
selection_reasoning: This fact explains the temporal relationship between temperature effects and observed disease cases, important for interpreting model-data comparisons.

fact: Maps of temperature suitability for Ross River virus transmission across Australia were generated by projecting R0 values onto high-resolution climate data.
source_span: To illustrate temperature suitability for RRV transmission across Australia , we mapped the number of months for which relative R0 ( T ) >0 and >0 . 5 for the posterior median , 2 . 5 and 97 . 5% credibility bounds for the full R0 model . We calculated R0 ( T ) at 0 . 2°C increments and projected it onto the landscape for monthly mean temperatures from WorldClim data at a 5 min resolution ( approximately 10 km2 at the equator ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact describes a key application of the model to visualize spatial and temporal transmission risk.

fact: The study calculated the basic reproduction number (R0) for mosquito-borne disease transmission across temperature gradients using high-resolution climate data.
source_span: We calculated R0 ( T ) at 0 . 2°C increments and projected it onto the landscape for monthly mean temperatures from WorldClim data at a 5 min resolution ( approximately 10 km2 at the equator ) .
selection_reasoning: Calculating R0 across temperature gradients is central to understanding how temperature affects disease transmission, a core scientific claim likely reflected in the abstract.

fact: The geographic area for climate data extraction was defined using the Global Administrative Boundaries Databases (GADM, 2012).
source_span: Climate data layers were extracted for the geographic area , defined using the Global Administrative Boundaries Databases (GADM , 2012 ) .
selection_reasoning: Defining the geographic scope is important background for interpreting the spatial modeling of disease transmission.

fact: The study used mosquito fecundity and adult survival data from McDonald et al. (1980) to fit thermal response models for mosquito traits.
source_span: The fecundity and adult survival data in McDonald et al . ( 1980 ) were published as time series of one experimental population at each temperature . The resulting data needed to be transformed to fit the corresponding trait thermal responses .
selection_reasoning: Using empirical data to fit thermal responses is a key methodological step supporting the study's main findings.

fact: Mosquito survival data were converted from percent surviving over time into lifespan data to fit thermal response models.
source_span: For survival , McDonald et al . reported the percent surviving approximately every other day ( hereafter: ‘semi-daily’ ) . We used these data—along with the number of female adults alive on the first day of oviposition at each temperature—to generate a semi-daily time series estimating the number surviving . To generate the dataset that we used to directly fit the thermal responses , we converted this time series into the number of female individuals who died on each day ( i . e . lifespan data ) .
selection_reasoning: Transforming survival data into lifespan data was necessary to model how temperature affects mosquito survival, a key trait influencing disease transmission.

fact: Mosquito fecundity data were adjusted by binning over the gonotrophic cycle and weighting by survival to better represent daily fecundity for thermal response fitting.
source_span: Because the population was synchronized , and because mosquitoes lay discrete clutches of eggs separated by several days ( the gonotrophic cycle duration ) , there were many data points when the populations did not produce offspring . These zero-inflated fecundity data are not ideal for fitting thermal responses . Therefore , after digitizing the semi-daily fecundity time series , we binned periods of several days ( the bin size varied by temperature , since the gonotrophic cycle duration varies with temperature ) and took a survival-weighted average within each bin ( so days with more individual mothers contributing to offspring production counted more ) . To generate the dataset that we used to directly fit the thermal responses , we weighted the values within each bin by the mean number of surviving mothers in that bin .
selection_reasoning: Adjusting fecundity data to account for mosquito reproductive cycles and survival improves the accuracy of thermal response models, which is central to the study's conclusions.

fact: The study used the genus name Aedes for mosquitoes despite a temporary taxonomic change to Ochlerotatus, reflecting current consensus.
source_span: In 2000 there was a proposed shift in mosquito taxonomy: several subgenera within the genus Aedes were elevated to genus status ( Wilkerson et al . , 2015 ) . This change affected Aedes vigilax and Aedes camptorhynchus , which were called Ochlerotataus vigilax and Ochlerotatus camptorhynchus for a time by some researchers . More recently , there has been a consensus to return to the previous naming system , so we use Aedes here , although many of the papers we cite use Ochlerotatus instead .
selection_reasoning: Clarifying mosquito taxonomy is important background for understanding the species studied and for consistency in interpreting results.

fact: Motor cortical beta oscillations have been observed for decades but their specific behavioral correlates remain unclear.
source_span: Motor cortical beta oscillations have been reported for decades , yet their behavioral correlates remain unresolved .
selection_reasoning: This background fact motivates the study and frames the research question about beta oscillations and behavior.

fact: Beta band oscillations (13–30 Hz) reliably emerge during specific motor actions such as isometric contraction, precision reaching, after movement-related cues, and prior to instructed reaches.
source_span: Beta band oscillations ( typically defined as 13–30 Hz ) have been noted to reliably emerge during specific motor actions such as isometric contraction and precision reaching , after movement-related cues , and prior to instructed reaches
selection_reasoning: This fact provides necessary background on when beta oscillations occur in motor behavior.

fact: The study used a novel neurofeedback task in which three macaque monkeys volitionally modulated their motor cortical beta oscillatory power before performing an arm reach.
source_span: To investigate how changes in population neural activity , beta oscillations , and behavior are linked , we recorded multi-scale neural activity from motor cortex while three macaques performed a novel neurofeedback task . Subjects volitionally brought their beta oscillatory power to an instructed state and subsequently executed an arm reach .
selection_reasoning: This describes the key experimental approach linking beta oscillations and behavior.

fact: Reaches preceded by a reduction in beta power had significantly faster movement onset times than reaches preceded by an increase in beta power.
source_span: Reaches preceded by a reduction in beta power exhibited significantly faster movement onset times than reaches preceded by an increase in beta power .
selection_reasoning: This is a principal behavioral finding linking beta oscillations to movement speed.

fact: Population neural activity shifted farther from a movement onset state during beta oscillations induced by neurofeedback or naturally occurring during reaching tasks.
source_span: Further , population neural activity was found to shift farther from a movement onset state during beta oscillations that were neurofeedback-induced or naturally occurring during reaching tasks .
selection_reasoning: This finding links beta oscillations to changes in neural population dynamics relevant to movement.

fact: The study establishes a population neural basis for slowed movement onset following periods of beta oscillatory activity.
source_span: This finding establishes a population neural basis for slowed movement onset following periods of beta oscillatory activity .
selection_reasoning: This is a key conclusion about the neural mechanism underlying the behavioral effect.

fact: Neurofeedback was used to manipulate beta oscillations in motor cortex to study their effects on arm reaching behavior.
source_span: This study uses neurofeedback to manipulate beta oscillations in subjects' motor cortices with the aim of studying effects on arm reaching .
selection_reasoning: This summarizes the main methodological innovation and purpose.

fact: Three macaque monkeys with chronic microwire electrode arrays implanted in their motor cortices were trained in a sequential neurofeedback and arm-reaching task.
source_span: In this study , three macaque monkeys with chronic microwire electrode arrays implanted in their motor cortices were trained in a sequential neurofeedback and arm-reaching task .
selection_reasoning: This fact describes the animal model and neural recording approach.

fact: Beta oscillations are interpreted as a measure of synchronization of underlying neural signals rather than as a causal signal influencing spiking activity via ephaptic effects.
source_span: Thus , in this study we interpret beta oscillations as a statistic of synchronization of the underlying neural signals , not as a signal that can independently and causally influence neural spiking via ephaptic effects .
selection_reasoning: This clarifies the conceptual framework for interpreting beta oscillations in the study.

fact: Prior studies showed that single motor cortical cells synchronize to ongoing beta oscillations but do not change their mean firing rate, though spiking variability decreases during oscillations.
source_span: Prior studies investigating neural activity changes during beta oscillations used acute , single-electrode recording preparations and showed that single cells are synchronized to ongoing oscillations but that the strength of this synchronization is unrelated to the involvement of the neuron during the motor task ( Murthy and Fetz , 1996a ) . These studies also show individual cells do not change their mean spike firing rate but do exhibit a reduction in spiking variability during oscillations compared to the variability exhibited before the oscillation ( Murthy and Fetz , 1996b ) .
selection_reasoning: This background fact helps contextualize the neural activity changes associated with beta oscillations.

fact: Beta oscillations in the 25–40 Hz range are a prominent feature of motor cortical activity during arm-reaching tasks in macaque monkeys.
source_span: A movement onset-aligned trial-averaged spectrogram from the intracortical recordings in contralateral motor and premotor cortex ( e . g . Monkey C in Figure 1d ) showed that the clearest movement-related desynchronization was in the 25–40 Hz band for all monkeys , consistent with early reports of beta oscillations in the macaque motor cortex ( Baker et al . , 1997; Murthy and Fetz , 1992 ) .
selection_reasoning: This background fact defines the relevant beta frequency band and establishes the biological basis for studying beta oscillations in motor cortex.

fact: The study trained three macaque monkeys to perform a center-out arm-reaching task and a novel sequential beta neurofeedback arm-reaching task to investigate how beta oscillations relate to motor behavior.
source_span: To explore how beta oscillations reflect changes in spiking activity and movement parameters , we trained three macaque monkeys to perform a typical center-out arm-reaching task ( CO task , Figure 1a ) , and a novel sequential beta neurofeedback arm-reaching task ( NR task , Figure 1b ) .
selection_reasoning: This describes the main experimental approach used to address the research question.

fact: During the neurofeedback-reaching task, monkeys modulated their motor cortical beta band power to control a cursor and achieve targets before performing reaching movements.
source_span: Subjects modulated endogenous motor cortical local field potential signals to move the vertical position of the beta cursor . Specifically , the cursor was controlled by a spectral estimate of beta band power normalized by a spectral estimate of broadband ( 1–100 Hz ) power ... When the beta cursor fell in the beta target , subjects were required to hold within the beta target for 450 ms . After successful completion , both the beta cursor and beta target disappeared , cueing that the reaching epoch had begun ... Subjects then executed a right-arm reach from the central target to a peripheral target to receive a liquid reward .
selection_reasoning: This fact summarizes the key method of neurofeedback used to link beta oscillations to motor behavior.

fact: Monkeys improved their ability to perform the beta neurofeedback task over about one week of training and achieved above chance performance during the neurofeedback epoch.
source_span: When monkeys were first exposed to the task , their time to successfully complete the neurofeedback epoch improved over days . After ~1 week of training per subject , performance plateaued and the beta power to cursor mapping was fixed ... During NR task performance from these days , subjects exhibited above chance performance ...
selection_reasoning: This fact shows that monkeys learned to volitionally modulate beta oscillations, supporting the study’s behavioral findings.

fact: The study found a neural population shift in motor cortex spiking activity that paralleled changes in motor behavior during neurofeedback-reaching tasks and was also observed during natural beta oscillations in reaching tasks.
source_span: Here , we report both changes in motor behavior following performance of neurofeedback during a sequential neurofeedback-reaching task , and a neural population shift that mirrors the observed change in motor behavior . Notably , this shift in neural population was also seen in naturally occurring beta oscillations during reaching tasks , suggesting that beta oscillations reflect a common signature of spiking patterns even in different task contexts .
selection_reasoning: This is a principal finding linking beta oscillations, neural population activity, and motor behavior.

fact: Beta oscillations in motor cortex may serve as a common neural signature encoding movement onset across different motor tasks.
source_span: This study ties together existing works on behavioral correlates of beta oscillations with hypotheses of how the motor cortex encodes movement onset through the lens of population-level neural activity .
selection_reasoning: This fact captures the study’s significance in understanding the functional role of beta oscillations in motor control.

fact: Monkeys were trained to control beta oscillatory power through a neurofeedback task, achieving stable performance after about one week of training.
source_span: When monkeys were first exposed to the task , their time to successfully complete the neurofeedback epoch improved over days . After ~1 week of training per subject , performance plateaued and the beta power to cursor mapping was fixed ...
selection_reasoning: This fact describes the training and stabilization of the neurofeedback task, a key method and prerequisite for the main findings.

fact: During the neurofeedback task, monkeys achieved above chance performance with average success rates of 60% and about 4 successful trials per minute.
source_span: During NR task performance from these days , subjects exhibited above chance performance ... Monkeys achieved average success rates of 60% and performed on average ~4 successful trials per minute .
selection_reasoning: This fact establishes that the monkeys successfully learned to modulate beta power, supporting the validity of the neurofeedback approach.

fact: The neurofeedback epoch successfully modulated beta power to different target levels, as shown by significant differences in normalized beta power at the go cue for the reaching epoch.
source_span: The neurofeedback epoch accomplished the goal of bringing beta power to different levels ... At the time of the go cue there is a significant group difference in normalized beta power for the four different neurofeedback target conditions ...
selection_reasoning: This fact is central to demonstrating that the neurofeedback task effectively controlled beta oscillations, a core experimental manipulation.

fact: Changes in beta power during neurofeedback were sometimes accompanied by opposite changes in low frequency power (1–10 Hz) in some monkeys.
source_span: In some subjects ( Monkeys C , G ) , increases and decreases in beta power were accompanied by reliable decreases and increases in low frequencies ( 1–10 Hz ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact highlights additional neural dynamics related to beta modulation, relevant for understanding the neurophysiological context.

fact: The percentage of time with beta oscillation bursts increased progressively from low to high beta targets during the neurofeedback epoch in all monkeys.
source_span: All subjects exhibit increasing percentages of on-beta time points for the low to high beta targets ...
selection_reasoning: This fact provides a time-domain confirmation that beta oscillations were effectively modulated, reinforcing the main neurofeedback manipulation.

fact: The neurofeedback epoch effectively increased or decreased beta oscillatory power prior to the arm-reaching epoch.
source_span: These three metrics ... demonstrate that the neurofeedback epoch served to increase and decrease beta oscillatory power prior to the arm-reaching epoch .
selection_reasoning: This fact summarizes the core experimental manipulation linking beta modulation to subsequent motor behavior.

fact: Increased beta oscillatory power prior to arm-reaching movements is associated with slower movement onset times in monkeys.
source_span: In all three animals, trials with high beta power targets had subsequent reaches with slower movement onset times (Figure 3a–c, two-tailed Cuzick’s test, Monkey S: z = 5.763, p=8.267e-09, n = 1183, Monkey C: z = 11.987, p<5e-20, n = 2168, Monkey G: z = 5.856, p=4.729e-09, n = 1028).
selection_reasoning: This is a principal finding linking beta power modulation to motor behavior, central to the study's main claim.

fact: Previous studies have found that increased beta power correlates with reduced movement onset speed, peak speed, and movement onset acceleration, but this study did not consistently find these effects across all subjects.

fact: Beta oscillations reflect a neural population state further from movement onset threshold, suggesting that beta oscillations favor a low-risk state preventing accidental movement initiation.
